I’m the founder & creative director at ✣HOVS, a studio that builds and runs its own products – and occasionally works with partners such as NASA/JPL to brand their space missions.

Currently growing mymind™, my peaceful escape from the chaos of the internet.

I’m also the co-founder of Semplice™ and Carbonmade™, which have been serving the creative community for more than two decades.

HOVS believes in brands and products that have a point of view.  Take a look at some of our work

↓

Tobias van Schneider

FOUNDER HOVS

HOVS — Building a retro-futuristic interpration of the original BMW airhead

Brand Identity, Product Design

In collaboration with my friend Seba (oneYedeer), we reimagined the classic BMW R100R airhead through a retro-futuristic lens. Every element, from the front fairing to the upholstery and tail, was custom-designed from the ground up. The bike maintains its clear identity as a BMW airhead, but with an unexpected twist that only those with a keen eye for design might fully appreciate.

View project details

Detail of the custom fabricated tail section

Custom badge design

NASA — Branding NASA’s mission to Jupiter’s icy moon, Europa

Brand Identity, Product Design

Once again, NASA asked HOVS to brand its latest mission to space – this time to find out if Jupiter’s moon, Europa, has habitable conditions for life. We designed the logo to reflect the clipper’s orbit of Jupiter, in which it will dip in and out of Jupiters' dangerous radiation zone to collect samples from the icy moon Europa. Another HOVS logo in space, 1.8 billion miles deep.

View project details

The mission type identifier on the launch rocket.

The additional text identifier.

mymind — Building a peaceful oasis within the chaos of the internet

Brand Identity, Product Design

mymind is the first and only extension for your real mind. It’s one private place to save everything you care about online, beautifully visualized and organized with the help of artificial intelligence. I co-founded mymind and manage the product design, branding and growth.

Visit mymind.com

A better place for everything.

The Thinking Guy: Our beloved mymind logo.

NASA — Designing an identity for the Mars 2020 Perseverance rover mission

Brand Identity, Product Design

For the 2020 Mars Rover launch, NASA commissioned HOVS to design a symbol celebrating both the legacy of space travel, and the energy of this new mission. At once the rover in abstract and blocks reaching to the sky, the logomark worked as well on NASA gear as it did on the rocket ship.

Visit the case study

The mission type identifier on the launch rocket.

The additional text identifier.

Semplice™ — The modern creative portfolio system with an old-school heart

Brand Identity, Product Design

The world's leading creatives use Semplice to build custom portfolios from scratch. I co-founded Semplice and I’m responsible for creative direction, product design, branding and marketing. It’s an ever-evolving tool, website backend and creative community helping designers build with pride.

Visit semplice.com

The Semplice Content Editor.

Featured Essays

from the DESK blog

Dear young Designer

Breaking the algorithm

Where are our design heroes?

AD ASTRA — A movie poster for Brad Pitt’s cinematic venture into deep space

Graphic Poster Design

The setting: deep space. The actor: Brad Pitt. The request: Design a poster for the film. Our work plays with white space and the acronym LOS, meaning Loss of Signal. While our designs were not ultimately the final poster, it was an honor to have our work considered for this film.

CARBONMADE — Helping creatives show off their work since 2005

Brand Identity, Product Design

Carbonmade is an institution in the creative community, powering more than 2 million portfolios since before Twitter and the iPhone existed. I came on board as partner in 2018 and led Carbonmade through a complete redesign and rebrand. I now manage Carbonmade’s product design and identity.

Visit carbonmade.com

Memomi — Reinventing the luxury shopping experience with a new high-end digital mirror

Advisor, Creative Director

Memomi created the world’s first digital mirror software platform called Memory Mirror. I overseeing the user experience, brand creative and ever-evolving product design. Memomi launched with partners such as Intel, IBM, Sony and Panasonic, and now appears in high-end stores like Neiman Marcus.

Visit memomi.co

3 ROOMS — Creating a transportive digital art gallery that celebrates the early internet

Brand, Storytelling, Webdesign

It started when we commissioned artist Jesperish to create three pieces of artwork incorporating the HOVS identity. Then it became bigger. We designed and built three rooms (works of art in themselves, in 40k pixel resolution) to feature each piece of art. Why? For pure fun & curiosity, like the good old days.

Brand Identity, Product Design

I worked for three years on the Spotify brand and product design, guiding Spotify through a major rebrand as the company tripled in size to more than 80 million users. I also worked on the Spotify Innovation Team, establishing and implementing Spotify’s first design guidelines and designing future products.

The Escape

Machine

a CUSTOM BMW R100R
made by HOVS & ONEYEDEER

Model: Shaye Murray

It all began with a photograph.

As I walked through the streets of Brooklyn I spotted a motorcycle parked on the street that caught my eye – a modified 1984 BMW R80.

Excited about the bike, I snapped a photo and showed it to an old friend, Matias Corea. Fate intervened when Matias revealed the builder of the motorcycle was his friend, Seba Achaval.

A connection was made, and a vision began to take shape.

Humble

Beginnings

The project started with a running 1984 BMW R80ST (which we ultimately switched to a R100R) – a solid donor bike that would soon prove to be just the beginning of a much grander transformation.

Anyone familiar with me knows I’m passionate about my work: every project must be a designed object, an art piece, a unique concept that performs as beautifully as it looks.

I imagined something that wouldn't feel too fabricated. It had to be handmade, something with charm, something with a unique personality and road presence.

Teaming up with Seba (oneYedeer) marked the beginning of a beautiful project and friendship.




The
inspiration

During the initial research phase, Seba discovered my stunning Mercedes 190E from 1989 with its distinctive warm metallic grey finish. An idea was born.

The car's angular lines, blocky headlights, and tail spoiler sparked an audacious idea. What if we created a "sacrilegious concept" by combining BMW and Mercedes design languages?

The proposal to use a Mercedes color on a BMW was unconventional, but we embraced the creative tension.

The Design
Evolution

The build began with a crucial upgrade to the front end. Rather than modify the original forks, we sourced a 2018 CBR1000RR front end, complete with Nissin calipers and Galfer rotors. This modern foundation would provide superior handling and braking while offering a more muscular aesthetic.

The tank position was modified by slanting it upwards with custom mounting points, creating both an aggressive stance and practical space for the updated electronics.


Seba continued with the experimentation using two 1970s KZ cowls to perfect the proportions. The goal was clear: create a sporty, aggressive solo-seater without leaning too much into common race bike aesthetics.

A defining design element emerged – a bold line running from front to back that inspired the tank's two-tone finish.

The upper section would wear the Mercedes paint code, while the lower portion would be finished in satin black, a theme that would extend to the front fairings and oil cooler.

The stark contrast between the Mercedes-inspired elements and the deep satin black powder coated framework created a sophisticated visual hierarchy.

This wasn't just about aesthetics. Every design choice served to enhance the riding experience, with the machinery receding into shadow beneath the rider's perspective.

Teaming up
with Myth Motors

The engine rebuild fell to our friend Matias at Myth Motors whose expertise with airheads proved invaluable. Matias’ focus when rebuilding engines is in longevity and reliability. The engine was a low mileage donor, but ran fine when the bike was acquired. The piston walls and the cylinder walls had little wear, so we decided to only replace the piston rings and con rod bearings.

All tile end gaskets and rubber parts were replaced. We refreshed the rear main seal, cleaned and inspected the oil pump with its o-ring, replaced the timing chain, crank nose seal, new clutch, and installed a new EME started motor mode more cranking power, less weight and less battery draw. 


Carburetors were rebuilt and rejetted to accommodate the switch from airbox to pods.

The transmission was completely overhauled and since it hadn’t seen any abuse, it only requested cleaning, new bearings, gaskets, seals, clips and springs. 

Modern upgrades included an airbox delete with a lithium Antigravity 8-cell battery installation, complete with custom cooling solutions and convenient charging access.

Custom
Fabrication

The subframe represents perhaps the most significant custom work, built around a 1½-inch steel main pipe extending from the center spine, reinforced with ¾-inch chromoly triangulated supports.

The riding position was completely reimagined, with the foot controls relocated to the passenger peg position and controls modified accordingly.

The seat base, constructed from fiberglass, was topped with carefully layered memory foam and wrapped in black Alcantara. 

The front fairing's centerpiece was produced in collaboration with our friend Marlon who took care of the 3D printing and refinements. We then paired it with a 1980s Jeep Wrangler headlight.

Custom brackets were fabricated to mount both the light and the 3D-printed fairing, which incorporated subtle aerodynamic elements inspired by Mercedes' design language.

The wiring harness was completely stripped out and replaced by a custom Motogadget Mo-Unit, eliminating the original fuse box, breakers, and relays.

A Chronoclassic 2 speedometer in black, M-switches, and fully adjustable billet aluminum clip-ons in anodized black completed the cockpit setup.

Custom controls included CBR1000RR aftermarket levers, braided hoses, and Rizoma reservoirs, all finished with custom machined aluminum bar ends.

In addition, we teamed up with jewelry designer Ashley Keeper on a fully custom tank emblem made out of bronze.

The tail section, featuring integrated LED lighting with running, brake, and turn signal functions, was laser-cut and welded in-house, completing the retro-future aesthetic.

The finished motorcycle represents more than just a custom build – it's a philosophical statement about breaking traditional boundaries in automotive design.

By merging Mercedes-Benz aesthetic elements with BMW mechanics, Seba created something entirely new while respecting both brands' heritage. The bike maintains its clear identity as a BMW airhead, but with an unexpected twist that only those with a keen eye for design might fully appreciate.

Thank you to everyone who's been involved in this project. Thank you Seba, Matias, Marlon, Ashley, Mark (BrooklynMoto), Rares, Andrew, Surya, Lizzy, Shaye, Barron and everyone else who's been involved over the past 2 years.

Thank you for

visiting the house.

About Alicia Zhou

I grew up in Fremont, California, where I spent most of my time between screens and sketchbooks. I love the feeling of turning vague ideas into something tangible. That instinct drew me to art first, and later to programming, which became another medium for building interactive, expressive work.

In my free time, you can often find me sketching my obsessions, making merch, or café hopping with friends. If you want to talk, collab, or just found a typo, feel free to say hi :)

TODD HAMILTON

I'm a product designer and developer with over 20 years of experience. I've designed products for billions of users at Facebook, where I spent a decade of my career. I'm passionate about prototyping and teaching other designers.

When I'm not in front of a screen, you'll find me surfing, golfing, or hanging out with family and friends. I live in Maine in a small town outside of Portland.

Today, I'm building AIProxy , a backend security tool that helps app developers protect API keys. AlProxy safely powers millions of AI requests per month and is used by thousands of developers.

“If a picture is worth 1000 words, a prototype is worth 1000 meetings.” - IDEO

I think about prototyping a lot and its a big part of my design process. I love this quote because I've always believed the best way to explore an idea is to prototype it. During my time at Facebook, I made hundreds of prototypes using various tools—for user research, demos, and presentations. They helped me communicate ideas more clearly, spark better conversations, and align people across the company in a way static designs never could.

Prototyping also opens the door to happy accidents. You stumble on interactions, animations, or flows you might never have uncovered if you were just designing static screens. Building and experimenting in motion invites discovery–and it's often in those small moments of play that the best ideas emerge.

CONTACT

I'm always looking for new opportunities to work on interesting projects. If you'd like to chat feel free to reach out.

Not a Number

Interactive blog posts on computer science and web development by Nanda Syahrasyad.

Subscribe

© 2021 - 2026

Interactive SVG Animations
An interactive course on making whimsical SVGs and SVG animations.
Build Your Own Database

October 21, 2025

How would you reinvent the database? In this post, we'll build a key-value database from the ground up.

A Deep Dive Into SVG Path Commands

July 3, 2023

The mystical d attribute in SVG paths is actually a series of small commands. In this guide, we'll take a look at each path command and how we can use them to draw icons.

The Power of Keys in Framer Motion

February 21, 2023

The React key prop is often only used to suppress React warnings, but it's actually a super powerful tool when used together with Framer Motion. In this post, we'll explore how to use it to make some pretty cool animations.

Inside Framer's Magic Motion

November 14, 2022

How does Framer Motion make layout changes look seamless? In this post, we're taking a deep dive into FLIP, the technique used by Framer Motion to animate changes in layout without sacrificing performance.

Rebuilding Babel: The Tokenizer

February 19, 2022

How do you build a modern JavaScript compiler from scratch? In this post, we'll rebuild the first piece of a compiler: the tokenizer.

How do Arrays Work?

November 12, 2021

What goes on under the hood of the most popular data structure? In this post, we'll uncover the secrets of the array by reinventing one ourselves.

Building a Debugger

May 14, 2021

If you want to build your own debugger, where would you start? In this post, we'll take a look at the inner workings of Playground — an online JS debugger.

The Sliding Window Pattern

March 20, 2021

An interactive look at a classic array algorithm pattern.

Input_002
Positioning
Adam Ho, I.S.P., is the independent studio practice of Adam Ho, a designer raised and based in Queens, New York. As a 1graphic designer and 2image maker, he places emphasis on delving into the nuances of 3protean, 4generative and 5intuitive brand identities, as well as showcasing those findings through exploratory interaction design and emerging media. His motivation for the practice is to 6research the interplay of art and design, taking notes and chords from different canons of the past, the present, and the interpretation of the future. This can be observed through his project, Liquidities, where creative expression and the ability to experiment with different approaches of art and technologies form a 7symbiotic relationship with his personal and commercial work.
          8Make it a bit different.

observations.title: Aruni — Design Collective
observations.text:
Aruni is a design collective that thinks, makes, breaks, and repeats.

Aruni is new. Our experience isn't. We're a senior design team solving real-world problems with simple, human-first solutions.

Book an intro call
Copy email

Why does design still matter?

In the AI era, functionality is baseline. When everything is "good enough," design becomes the advantage.

Personalization drives retention. Empathy builds trust. Design turns intelligent systems into products people choose and pay for.

How can we help?

We partner with teams and founders across brand sprints, web and product design, motion, and social assets, shaping cohesive digital experiences from strategy to execution.

From defining visual systems to designing end-to-end digital products, we support you at every stage of your brand and product journey.

How do we work?

From kickoff to handoff, we move fast and stay aligned at every step.

We clarify what needs to be built, who it's for, and why it matters. Then we define a clear direction, design every screen and state, refine the details, and deliver work that's ready to launch and scale.

We share progress updates 2–3 times a week.

How do we price?

We keep things simple and flexible. Work with us on a monthly subscription you can pause or cancel anytime, or collaborate on a project when it makes sense.

*Aruni is light, the first glimpse of something new.

designer. creative. curiousista.

Living my childhood dream in San Francisco

I love making digital things feel more human. Things that do their job, make human life a tad bit easier, make the world aesthetically pleasing

I design for the joy of giving, because people are wonderfully complicated. We are curious, tired, skeptical, sentimental, impatient, playful, easily confused, and capable of being changed, slightly, by the smallest interruption. 

The way I work is mostly noticing, collecting, making, doubting, remaking, and detail-wrestling until the complicated thing starts to feel simple. I care about finesse: 
 the touch, the timing, the small decision that makes the hard thing feel easy.

observations.title: Tesla for Business — Pranshu Agarwal
observations.text:
Home
Tesla for Business

One operating layer for businesses buying, managing, and integrating Tesla products

Project website
Tesla For Business
Role
Lead product designer
Timeline
2022–2024
Product type
B2B Product Suite

Tesla for Business Website

Tesla already had a mature ownership model for individual customers. Businesses introduced a more complex relationship: the company buying a Tesla product might not be the company managing it, the person using it, or the party paying for its service, charging, or subscriptions.

I helped evolve Tesla for Business from an early fleet-management product into a scalable B2B platform spanning registration, ordering, fleet operations, service, charging, billing, developer access, and future Tesla product categories.

The deeper design challenge was to make those relationships work across thousands of products, multiple companies, many user roles, and different countries—without rebuilding the platform every time Tesla introduced something new.

Reading control

How much do you want to read?

The whole spiel
<8 minutes

What

I grew with the product from early infrastructure to platform strategy

A complete operating layer for Tesla’s business customers

Tesla for Business is the software relationship between Tesla and organizations that buy and operate Tesla products.

My work covered the complete ownership lifecycle: registration, onboarding, ordering, delivery, fleet management, users and permissions, payments, service, charging, subscriptions, Fleet API, developer applications, and Tesla Shop for Business.

The same framework was designed to expand beyond passenger vehicles into Semi, charging infrastructure, energy products, autonomous fleets, and future Tesla categories.

One operating layer across Tesla products, infrastructure, autonomy, energy, and AI.
I grew with the product from early infrastructure to platform strategy

I first joined the work during my 2022 internship, extending the young fleet product with Tesla Shop for Business and the first Tesla Semi customer infrastructure for the Pepsi and Frito-Lay rollout.

When I returned full-time, my role expanded into end-to-end product design and foundational platform strategy across the business relationship.

Built for first 100 Tesla Semitrucks.
My first Tesla project - Tesla for Business Shop
Why

Research had to extend beyond the purchaser

Business ownership is a network, not an account

For an individual customer, ownership can often be represented as Person → Product.

For a business, the same Tesla might involve one company purchasing it, another company operating it, an administrator managing access, a fleet manager maintaining it, a driver using it, separate parties paying for charging and service, and a third-party application accessing its data.

All of those relationships can change independently—then multiply by thousands of products.

Who owns this product, who manages it, who uses it, and who is responsible for what?

The platform needed to outlive the vehicle-first mental model

Vehicles dominated Tesla’s business, so the early software naturally thought in terms of vehicles, VINs, and drivers. But a platform designed too specifically around passenger vehicles would force every new business line to create another account and management experience.

I pushed the model toward reusable concepts: product, organization, manager, user, permission, and responsibility. A Model Y, Semi, charger, or future Tesla product could inherit the same foundational relationships while exposing its own operational capabilities.

We designed around relationships, not products.

Research had to extend beyond the purchaser

I spoke with teams at Hertz to understand large-fleet operations, but some of the most useful research happened further downstream. The person living with many product decisions was often the driver—not the purchaser or fleet administrator.

I started taking Teslas as Ubers and talking directly with drivers about fleet access, charging, service, and ownership. It made the distinction between customer, administrator, and end user tangible rather than theoretical.

Historical usage, operational data, customer conversations, and product judgment shaped the first release; real production use became our highest-fidelity usability environment.

I took Teslas as Ubers to learn from the drivers living with fleet decisions every day.
How

New products extended the platform instead of creating new accounts

Registration established the organization before the fleet

Tesla for Business begins before a company owns a Tesla product. I designed the registration experience end to end: account request, contact details, business information, and verification documents.

The flow established who was requesting access, which business they represented, how that company intended to work with Tesla, and whether the organization could be verified. This created the identity layer everything else depended on.

Once registered, the organization could add people and assign different levels of access—because “business user” was never a single role.

Registration established who was requesting access, which company they represented, and whether it could be verified.
Approval connected the organization to Tesla for Business—from email to terms to first access.
Permissions followed responsibility

Roles gave us a starting point, but the more interesting layer was responsibility at the product level. The person managing a product might not be the person paying for it.

A vehicle could be owned by one organization, managed by another, used by a driver, charged by the company, and serviced under a different responsibility. Fleet management therefore supported assignments across organizations and individuals.

Product-level responsibilities separated company assignment, vehicle management, drivers, upgrades, and order history.
Learn more: One product, several responsibilities
The information architecture followed the ownership lifecycle

Customer conversations consistently followed the same sequence: I want to buy → I want to manage → I need service → I need account and operational controls.

That became Orders / Fleet / Service / Shop / Developer / Account. The product could grow without asking customers to understand Tesla’s internal organization.

Orders carried a business through configuration, purchasing, delivery details, PO information, driver assignment, payment responsibility, VIN fulfillment, and delivery tracking. Once delivered, each product entered Fleet—the operational center for what a business owned and what it could do with it.

Orders, Fleet, Service, Shop, Developer, and Account followed the customer’s ownership lifecycle.
Make selection powerful; keep actions simple

A fleet manager rarely struggles to understand an action like assign driver, change payer, or buy subscription. The difficult question is: Which 437 products should this apply to?

I focused the interaction complexity on making selection fast, precise, and trustworthy. Users could combine product, geography, company, user, operational state, service state, financial responsibility, and other metadata, then apply a predictable bulk action to the result.

Saved groups and filters allowed repeat operational tasks to scale from one Tesla product to thousands without rebuilding the same selection every time.

Selection did the hard work: choose the right vehicles, then apply one predictable bulk action.
Learn more: The enterprise-scale tradeoff
Service became an operational workflow, not a table column

Service information originally appeared as another column in Fleet. Operators could technically see a product was in service, but the interface did little to explain what needed to happen next.

I designed a dedicated Service dashboard around meaningful status—especially Needs Attention / Action and Ready for Pickup. The hierarchy reflected urgency instead of asset structure and reduced the gap between a state changing and the customer acting on it.

That work exposed the need for a broader notification framework: a tray, in-app messages, cadence-based reminders, escalating alerts, and communication at company, manager, and end-user levels.

Service became a dedicated operational dashboard organized around status and urgency.
Appointment details surfaced concerns, contacts, and timing without losing fleet context.
Fleet API extended Tesla into the customer’s own software

Large operators already had operational software. Tesla for Business did not need to replace every fleet-management system; it needed to let those systems connect securely to Tesla.

I designed the new developer product from the ground up, including registration, application management, scopes, authorization, billing, usage, and developer administration.

Scopes made access intentional. A developer application should not inherit every capability simply because a business authorized it. Access needed to describe the relationship, not just the account.

Product education and usage-based pricing led into a guided Fleet API access request.
Applications made authorization explicit, then kept credentials and scopes manageable in one place.
New products extended the platform instead of creating new accounts

Tesla Semi was an early test. Its buyers, operators, and expectations differed from passenger vehicles, but the underlying relationship remained recognizable: organization, products, users, permissions, service, charging, and payments.

Charging infrastructure raised the same questions again: who owns the charger, who manages it, who accesses its data, who pays, and who responds when it needs maintenance?

The direction became clear: fleet management should eventually mean Tesla product fleet management—not only vehicle management.

Commercial charging, live fleet data, maps, and product-level controls extended the same platform beyond passenger vehicles.
Impact

Ownership became more sophisticated without changing its foundation

The foundation is still absorbing new business models

The strongest evidence of success is not one launch metric. It is that the underlying model continues to expand.

Business ordering, driver assignment, delegated fleet management, charging and service payer assignment, subscriptions, recalls, commercial charging, developer roles, and third-party access all build on the same primitives: organizations + users + products + roles + responsibilities.

The platform became self-evolving: new capabilities could attach to the system rather than requiring another silo.

Tesla for Business became the front door for vehicles, Semi, commercial charging, energy, and partner services.

Fleet API became a commercial platform of its own

What began as a new API-access experience grew into Tesla’s official Fleet API ecosystem, supporting pay-per-use billing, developer application management, usage limits, and Fleet Telemetry.

The developer surface became both an interface and infrastructure layer—evidence that the original foundation could support an ongoing commercial platform.

Ownership became more sophisticated without changing its foundation

Tesla now publicly supports one company owning a vehicle while another manages it. Managing companies can administer drivers, charging, service, and subscriptions for assigned products.

The platform also supports distinct Admin, Developer, Finance, Fleet, Order, Fulfillment, and Service roles without forcing every user to inherit every part of that complexity.

What I took from it

The durable outcome was the foundation, not any one screen

Comment
C
Enterprise complexity lives in the relationships surrounding every action

Tesla for Business changed how I think about enterprise design. The complexity did not come from any individual workflow; it came from the relationships surrounding every action.

Who owns something? Who can use it? Who manages it? Who pays for it? Who is allowed to change it? Once those relationships were modeled well, individual features became much easier to build.

The durable outcome was the foundation, not any one screen

The more important design outcome was not a dashboard, API flow, or service screen. It was a foundation that could keep answering those questions as Tesla’s products, customers, and business models evolved.

The platform started by managing fleets of vehicles. I designed it to eventually manage fleets of Tesla products.

observations.title: NDR | Product Designer
observations.text:
Hi, I'm Gianluca Andrisani

Designer & Engineer at Customuse

I thrive at the intersection of design, engineering, and product. Where vision meets execution to craft bold, intuitive experiences that people love.

Work
About
Playground
A Hyrox mobile app that I designed and built

Rounds started with a personal need: training for HYROX when organised classes no longer fit around work. This is the story of how I shaped that need into a product, moving between Figma and Codex to explore ideas, build them, and refine how they look and feel.

Training on my own

I started training for HYROX through organised classes. When work got busier, I could no longer make the scheduled sessions. I still wanted to train, but doing it alone meant figuring out the workout, the movements, and the timing myself.

I wanted to arrive at the gym after work and get going: choose a suitable workout, follow visual guidance through the session, and eventually see whether I was improving. That everyday situation became the reference point for the product.

Thinking through making

I built Rounds to help me train for HYROX on my own. It became a project in which I could move between product thinking, visual exploration, and engineering, using Figma and Codex to turn an idea into something I could use, question, and refine.

Making the first idea tangible

I started with a product where people could create their own workouts, remix existing ones, and run a timed session. Building that first prototype in Codex made the idea tangible, but it also exposed how much planning I was asking someone to do before they could train.

Designing for someone already at the gym

In Figma, I stepped back to think about the experience I wanted. I explored a directory of workouts and different ways to organise the homepage. But picturing someone standing in the gym, ready to train, helped me narrow the scope. Creating and remixing workouts still asked people to plan before they could train.

The homepage became a welcome, one clear “Choose workout” action, and recent workouts. Browsing and saved workouts belonged in the picker. The concepts show that exploration, including the directory and two approaches to a more focused home.

Building a world around the workout

I wanted Rounds to carry some of the intensity and roughness of HYROX, while feeling dynamic and visually distinctive. I explored realistic gym scenes. But it felt really bland and boring, so I jumped into Pinterest to gather inspiration.

Generating imagery was an art-direction process: choosing the framing, judging the physical effort and movement, and refining the treatment across the collection. I used Figma to see how that world worked as an interface, then brought it into the app to evaluate it alongside real content and interactions. All of it was done in Codex.

From a composition to an interaction

The workout details sheet is a good example of how I moved between tools. I set its initial vision in Figma because it was the fastest way to explain the composition in detail. Once it was implemented with Codex, I refined its movement, transitions, and feel in code.

Working with the live interaction made the next decisions concrete: how a progress card should expand within the sheet, when its text should disappear and return, and how to get back to the workout. Preferences followed a similar process, with the sheet changing size as content moved between views. Screenshots established the direction; using the app exposed what still felt wrong.

Finding the feel of a simple choice

Choosing how often to train was another interaction shaped in both Figma and Codex. I designed the first iteration in Figma: a large number, a slider, and a simple question about the rhythm that fits your week.

The polish and final iterations happened directly in Codex. Working with the running app let me refine how the number, colour, and movement responded to the slider, then try the interaction again. The recordings show that choice in onboarding and in preferences: the initial composition came from Figma, while its final feel emerged through iteration in code.

Deciding what progress means

Analytics developed through building. I started by asking what would be valuable to track, then worked with Codex to define what improvement meant across different workouts: completing the same work faster, or completing more exercises within a fixed time. Unfinished exercises and partial reps would not count.

Seeing the first implementation made me question whether the information was useful enough to deserve its own tab. I drafted alternatives in Figma, built them, and tried again. I wanted one understandable trend across my training, supported by concrete improvements within individual workouts. That led to a performance index based on comparable attempts and personal baselines.

The place and moment mattered too. The analytics tab could show the broader trend; workout details could hold deeper history. Immediately after training, a short recap could tell me how I did against my first and previous attempts. The calculations and the presentation evolved together.

The small details

A lot of the work happened in the small details: how a sheet opens, how a number responds to a slider, and how progress appears after a session. I kept returning to these moments in the running app, adjusting the movement, timing, and visual treatment until they felt right together.

These close-ups bring those decisions into focus. Figma helped me establish the direction; iterating directly in Codex let me try the details in motion and refine how they felt to use.

Taking ownership of the engineering

I worked with Codex throughout the engineering process, setting the direction and questioning the implementation as it developed. I would describe the behaviour I wanted, work through the proposed approach, and ask how the pieces connected before moving ahead. My role was to understand the system well enough to make those decisions, rather than judge the result only by what appeared on screen.

I used that back-and-forth to explore tradeoffs, challenge assumptions, and revisit choices as the product changed. When something felt wrong, I pushed past the visible symptom to understand its cause. Codex helped me investigate and implement changes; I assessed whether they solved the problem and what they meant for the rest of the app.

Testing the app on the phone kept that work grounded. I checked how changes behaved in use, questioned fixes that introduced other problems, and kept refining until the implementation supported the experience I wanted.

Tools change, iteration doesn't

Different questions needed different ways of working. Sometimes I needed a Figma composition to make the vision clear. Sometimes I needed working code to discover whether an idea was useful. And sometimes a detail that felt wrong on the phone led me into the architecture underneath it.

Codex helped me build and investigate quickly, while I kept directing the product, the aesthetic, and the decisions about what to keep.

In the end, as we all hold strong opinions regarding the tools, what stands out to me is the importance and sameness of the process. I moved between tools, but the questions and iterations were consistent, without ever settling with the first result, but always asking what could be better. This is what makes us designers, obsessing over surface areas and interactions, and what makes us engineers, obsessing over the systems that support them.

Trickpad — macOS gesture utility

2026

I built Trickpad so I could control dictation and other writing actions without needing to touch my keyboard. It maps Magic Mouse and Magic Trackpad gestures to keyboard shortcuts, system actions, URLs, and scripts, including different bindings for individual apps.

I already used dedicated apps for window management and automation, so I didn’t want another large utility. Trickpad acts as a lighter connection to those tools through their existing hotkeys and deep links. Its complete configuration lives in a readable, plain-text TOML file, which makes the setup easy to inspect, back up, and maintain with a coding agent.

I soon decided to flesh it out as a public product. That pushed me to account for workflows beyond mine, including trackpad edge and corner clicks, macOS gesture conflicts, system controls, and apps that interpret synthesized shortcuts differently. I also built the documentation, agent-guided setup, packaging, updates, icon, storefront, and product site needed for it to stand on its own.

Wedding invitations and site

Julia & Thelxinoe, 2026

Invitation suite and website for a friend's wedding, built out from a shared moodboard of illuminated manuscripts, medieval tapestry, and tattoo flash. The save-the-date artwork became the site's hero, rebuilt in CSS so the J and X tiles fade into an arc under two layered radial-gradient masks, with soft parallax over it. The invitations came last and are their own drawing, taking only the deep purple and gold of the site's later sections.

Julia is a backend developer and had already wired an RSVP flow to a Google Sheet through Apps Script, where guests looked up their party across several pages. I rebuilt it as a single surface that prefetches the whole guest list on open, so searching is instant and one person can answer for everyone in their party. Filling it out went from about 18 seconds to 9 in my own testing.

This website — Content system & frontend

2025

I built this site after growing tired of fitting my portfolio into static site builders and general-purpose CMSs. I wanted direct control over how the work is organized, presented, and connected, without treating every unconventional interaction as a workaround.

The site began as a Next.js frontend with content in Sanity and media in Cloudinary. In 2026, I consolidated it into one codebase so written content now lives as MDX files alongside the application, while images and videos live in a single Cloudflare R2 bucket. Content changes travel through the same review and deployment process as code, and the files remain readable in Obsidian and by coding agents.

The homepage supports three views of the same work: a visual grid, a project list, and an overview of past roles. Filters and active views persist in the URL for shareability, while direction-aware transitions preserve a sense of spatial continuity between them.

I built the surrounding content system to support custom article layouts, shared media metadata, automatic video derivatives, and Markdown versions of the public pages for AI agents.

Building the portfolio in code also made polishing it more enjoyable. Instead of moving between Figma and an approximation of the final interface, I created a /lab section where I can experiment directly with the real components. While working with Claude and Codex, I can turn an idea such as animation timing, shader behavior, spacing, or visual treatment into a set of controls, compare variations in context, and carry the values I choose back into the site.

A range of design work across our product, website, and supporting systems.

My initial sales and support role gave visibility into where users were experiencing confusion. That shaped what I built next: walkthrough videos and tutorials, new product and support pages, and a reimagining of our flagship product. The redesign proposes replacing its menu-driven interface with a guided workflow built from interface primitives, grounded in Microsoft’s WinUI guidelines.

I also shaped the design on a website refresh, working with an external agency on the wireframes and content restructuring. After their handoff I kept iterating on the visual side, polishing colors, diagrams, and layouts.

Most recently, the role has grown to include some of the underlying systems engineering myself.

Slumber Game Development

”Videogame Design and Development” course led by Christopher Weaver, 2019

An iOS game prototype that turns sleep science into a playable 3D world for kids. I pitched the concept and was elected to lead a team of four to build it in a double-credit software development intensive at Wesleyan, run by the founder of Bethesda Softworks.

The game maps the brain's sleep stages to an adventure (keeping neurons firing, clearing toxins, repairing systems, and synthesizing memory), so kids learn the science by playing. I led production and set the art direction, designed level structure, cleaned and UV-mapped meshes, and built motion graphics for the teaser and keynote.

We took the concept from pitch to alpha, user-tested it with kids at a local elementary school, and delivered the final pitch to industry judges from AFI, Harmonix, Warner Bros. Games, and Demiurge Studios. They awarded us first place for "most original concept and execution" and "highest quality business presentation."

Robin Goes Outside Short Film

Wesleyan College of Film and the Moving Image, 2020

Wesleyan’s film studies program is centered on theory and form analysis, but for my thesis I opted to make a short film (one of 21 made that year). I wrote, directed, and edited an 11-minute production with a 16-person crew across 40 hours of shooting and a $2,800 crowdfunded budget.

I took cues from Krisha and Punch-Drunk Love, letting energetic camerawork and sound design carry much of the opening without dialogue.

A jury of 5 film professors (including AFI board emeritus Jeanine Basinger) and 3 anonymous Hollywood professionals awarded my film with honors and the Frank Capra Prize “for creating a senior film that is fully cinematic and uses the tools of filmmaking at the highest level,” and for “exemplifying Capra’s skill in telling a human story that contains both humor and pathos.”

Small, family-run B2B software company. Users include Eli Lilly, 3M, EPA, and hundreds of labs, plants, and businesses around the world. I've been here since 2021 in a part-time but wide-ranging role that started in sales and customer support, then gradually grew to cover design, documentation, and lately engineering work I've taken on myself.

Early on, being the primary person hearing what confused our users meant I knew where the product was hard to understand. That shaped what I built afterwards: videos and guides that cut recurring setup questions by about 30%, new product and support pages, and a concept redesign of the interface aimed at what users found most confusing.

I migrated our internal customer database off a 25-year-old Access setup that vendors had quoted us $25–60k to rebuild for years. I built it on Next.js + Supabase with a phased migration plan so the legacy system remains editable while a properly relational model grows underneath. I also rebuilt our customer-facing support docs on an AI-legible, file-first platform (Mintlify), with a pipeline that migrated hundreds of articles off WordPress. The new platform lets AI agents easily receive context about our products and makes our docs easier to update and extend.

Business & Product Fellowship

2023 - 2025

Venture for America / Ember

Two-year national fellowship for recent grads building careers at growing companies (~10% acceptance rate).

Their two-week business development intensive featured workshops from McKinsey, IDEO, and Frog Design, ending with a 3-day design sprint where I led a team to both Judge's Pick and Crowd Favorite for the design and presentation of my product idea.

I also co-organized Philly Phormal — VFA's flagship 500-person community event, run by fellows during the program's wind-down.

Designer

2023 - 2024

Foundation Studio

Contract role with a small studio that worked with Techstars startups and other early-stage founders on their pitches. I spent about a year designing decks for three of them, sharpening positioning and competitive differentiation and finding ways to make their ideas land clearly with investors.

A lot of the work was putting words and visual narratives to compelling ideas founders hadn't quite expressed in their existing materials about what their product really was, or where they wanted to take it. I also built a small React/Next.js form tool for another client's internal workflow.

Brand and Web Designer (Webflow)

2022 - 2022

Rices Mill Booksellers

Built and designed a Webflow website and brand refresh for a small business serving school district administrators.

ACT Tutor

2022 - 2022

Summit Educational Group

Provided personalized 1:1 virtual ACT tutoring to high school students, creating customized study plans to help improve their test scores.

Producer's Assistant / Video Editor

2021 - 2021

Dreamatorium Productions

Enhanced virtual event accessibility for new Sign Language play through custom video graphics and multiple interpreter feed integration. Collaborated with sign language consultants to optimize digital solutions for Deaf attendees.

Video Editor

2021 - 2021

"And We're Live" web series

Salvaged scrappy footage and audio into a coherent narrative, 40-min pilot episode for web series "And We're Live," making savvy changes to the tone, pacing, and dialogue of scenes as needed to solve production-related errors and technical issues.

Brand / Web Designer and Video Editor

2020 - 2021

Berkshire Playwrights Lab

Started in administrative support for a small theatre and arts nonprofit and grew the role with design and digital work as the org pivoted to virtual programming during COVID. Redesigned their website (doubled traffic), refreshed their visual identity for better scaling across digital surfaces, and designed assets and helped run seven virtual events.

Writer / Director / Editor

2019 - 2020

"Robin Goes Outside" Short Film

Wrote, directed, and edited an 11-minute thesis film at Wesleyan, managing a 16-person crew and $2,800 crowdfunded budget across 40 hours of shooting. Collaborated with student artists on the score, titles, and promotional materials; edited 400+ assets in Final Cut Pro, creating an eccentric and intense atmosphere drawn from Krisha and Punch-Drunk Love.

The film won the Frank Capra Prize, awarded for blending humor with pathos and "using the tools of filmmaking at the highest level."

Project Manager / Producer / Pitch Speaker

2019 - 2019

Slumber Development Team

Pitched an original concept for an educational iOS game teaching sleep cycles and brain science to elementary schoolers, and was elected to lead one of four teams in a double-credit software development intensive run by the founder of Bethesda Softworks.

Over the semester I served as project manager, art director, and pitch lead. I wrote design documentation, coordinated artists and programmers using Agile methods, and delivered a final pitch to industry judges from AFI, Harmonix, Warner Bros. Games, and Demiurge Studios. They awarded us first place for "most original concept and execution" and "highest quality business presentation."

Graphic Design Intern

2016 - 2017

Amazi Food Company

Proposed a new brand and graphic identity to better express the startup's health and ethics approach in the snack industry. Created signs, sell sheets and merchandising designs.

Bachelor of Arts

2016 - 2020

Wesleyan University

Film Studies major and Digital Design minor.

Film and media: Narrative Complexity in Television, Television Aesthetics, World Cinema History, Hollywood Film History, Film Production, Screenwriting, Television Writing, Videogames as Moving Image, American Film Comedy, Film Business.

Design and computation: Video Game Design and Development, Functional Programming (Pyret), Creative Coding (Processing), Graphic Design for the Web, Data Visualization (R), Participatory Design, Digital Art, Digital Photography.

Humanities: Modern Aesthetic Theory, Creative Writing for New Media, American Studies, Linguistics, Cultural Anthropology, Social Psychology.

Co-designed and led a semester-long student forum on the aesthetics and history of teen television.

[ 01 ] Intro

Hi, I'm Shaahid. I'm a designer and developer who
enjoys building interfaces, improving existing
products, and turning designs into fast, well-built
frontends.

[ 02 ] Approach

I look for what's holding a product back, whether it's
confusing UX, inconsistent visuals, or an interface
that feels unfinished. Then I redesign and build it
around what actually matters: making the
experience clearer, smoother, and more useful.

[ 03 ] Now

I run StillMotion, an independent studio helping
early-stage startups and brands turn their ideas into
polished digital experiences, along with this I am
looking for an internship with a team where I can get
better at what I do.

Lué Studio® is an end-to-end, powerhouse
in digital design, development and direction.
Our work encompasses brand and identity, websites and user interfaces, motion and experience, strategy and positioning — all anchored by
powerful storytelling. We think that last one is the most important.
By blending unbridled creative flair with meticulous technical rigour,
we craft user journeys that captivate and resonate.
It's no secret that we live and breathe digital experiences.
Like the alchemists of old, our goal is simple yet ambitious: to transform
the ordinary into the extraordinary — turning base metal into pure gold.

observations.title: Curiosity: Daniel White
observations.text:
Daniel White
Music box
Curiosity

Chapter the First

Curiosity

In which a boy of eleven takes the computer apart, and is not sorry.

C:\>
Plate I. The machine on the desk, with its case off.

Iwas eleven years of age when I first wished to know what went on inside the machine on our desk. Nobody could tell me, and so I set about finding out.

It was not only computers. I wanted to know how everything worked, and I was never content with the outside of a thing. I went looking underneath, at the code and the engineering and the reasons.

Before long I had built a search engine of my own, upon Google’s search API. After it came a physics engine for two-dimensional games, written in Java, wherein small bodies fell and bounced as they ought. The figure below is a small tribute to it.

Fig. 1. Small bodies, falling and bouncing as they ought. Drop another

or press anywhere on it

I kept learning because I enjoyed it, and because I wished to be very good at it. I still do.

Diego Schwertberger is a designer with Latin American roots based in Vienna, Austria. After an exchange in Milano, he moved back to his hometown Vienna, where he now lives and works, while finishing his BA in Fashion Design at University of Applied Arts Linz. Diego has been working as designer and consultant with and for a wide range of clients in the creative sector. Among other features, his work was shortlisted in the Venus Beyond category by the Creative Club Austria. In April of 2026 he debuted on the runway showing a capsule collection at Chile Fashion Week in Santiago.

2026

Earlier this year I started working for Bueronardin in Vienna, while working on my graduate collection, which will be shown at a Fashion Show in Vienna, in the beginning of June.

In April of this year I debuted showing a capsule collection during Chile Fashion Week 2026 in Santiago de Chile.

2025

From March until July I did my Erasmus Exchange Semester at NABA focusing on knitwear design and the developement of a knitwear collection.

After nearly two years at Grafik Apartment, I now work as Freelance Designer, while working on my Final Bachelor Collection.

2024
2024

In January of this year I started a new job as Graphic Designer at Grafik Apartment while still working Freelance and studying Fashion & Technology at University of Arts Linz. In August I had the opportunity of an one month internship at austrian designer Christina Seewald.

2023

After a semester at KMD Herbststraße the educational interests changed and the next step was to enrol in the University of Arts Linz and begin studying Fashion & Technology.

Later this year the private and educational setting changed from Vienna to Upper Austrian City Linz, where I also worked as a freelance Graphic Designer.

2022
2022

With the beginning of February, I got a position as a Social Media Manager at zone14, an Austrian sports-tech start-up. After graduating with my BA from the New Design University in June, I began working at PR firm LOEBELL NORDBERG and quickly moved to INNER, the subsidiary focusing on Experiential Publicity with clients such as H&M, NeueHoheit or Rosewood Vienna. Later on, I enrolled at the KMD Herbststraße for a diploma Fashion, which started in Fall.

2021

In this years summer I worked three months as Graphic Design intern at PEACH Wien. Clients during this period included Albertina, European Chamber Music Academy and Mark Pock.

2020

The renowned Club Lauchos Vienna FC was founded. A short but successful chapter in football history begins.

2019

In October of 2019 I started my Graphic- and Information Design education at New Design University St. Pölten.

2017

In July of this year, after six years of traveling, singing and many unforgetable memories I finished my school education. The following six months I completed the social service at Caritas Wien.

2011
2011

Thanks to an early interest and talent in music in 2011 the Vienna Boy’s Choir got a new member joining them for three incredible years full of travelling the world and singing on stage in front of an audience of several thousands of people.

2009

In the early days of my football career I played as a goalkeeper. The team never really succeeded. For good reasons I then switched to playing as a defender and midfielder. The look sums up my goalkeeping career.

2002

The first introduction to Sony’s PlayStation 2. But the resolution these days really wasn’t it.

Mercedes-Benz Avantgarden

Project work completed during my employment at Grafik Apartment.

AVANTGARDEN by Mercedes-Benz was an experiental event in October 2024 at Museum Angerlehner in Austria. There, visitors got the opportunity to explore the newest innovations in Mercedes-Benz EQ, AMG and Maybach models.

The logo design incorporates abstract shapes inspired by the fusion of avant-garde artistry and garden aesthetics. Each element, derived from the deconstruction of the AVANTGARDEN wordmark, symbolizes sculptures, hedges, and architectural structures—creating a balanced visual that represents the event’s focus on continuity and innovation.

The logo is completed with the Mercedes-Benz Star, corporate font, and the distinctive Avantgarden Green.

observations.title: Ìní·Olúwa
observations.text:
ÌníOlúwa Abíódún

AI-fluent designer shipping products and growing the design functions behind them.

I’m currently the Lead Product Designer at AirOps, where I lead design for Quill, our agent captain, across Playbooks, Grids, and Brand Kit.

Before that, I led design for AI growth at Intercom, across Fin Studio, Fin Voice, fin.ai, and the self-serve business. Prior, I was Principal Product Designer at Norton (Gen Digital), where I owned the design function across 58 EMEA and Rest of World markets.

I’m a builder, and I’m good at growing teams and helping them raise the bar on what customers experience and, most importantly, enjoy the process of making.

I write In Good Company, notes on the blurry edges of design, code, and strategy, and run Designers Building Cool Shit, a London demo night for designers building with AI.

Origin

ÌníOlúwa means “God’s precious one”, a name from the Yorùbá tribe of South Western Nigeria.

I grew up in Ìbàdàn, moved to Johannesburg and have lived in London for several years. Nigeria gave me resourcefulness. South Africa gave me resilience. The UK gave me rigour and access.

I trained as a lawyer from 15 and was called to the Bar at 21. At 16, I ran a couture label that won a national competition from 62 designers — handstitching hundreds of petals with over 20,000 sand beads for a dress worn by actress Dakore Akande at the AMVCAs.

Law. Couture. Product design. The through-line is the same: make the thing, make it well, ship it into the world. Law taught me to write for the hostile reader and argue the other side first; couture taught me the detail is the product. Both turned out to be AI-era design training.

More than a decade on, I’ve shipped products and led teams across AI, cybersecurity, fintech, hiring, and social communities.

we looked at several design agencies, but really happy we went with lowercase. what sets them apart is their willingness to pivot when something isn't working - no ego, just results. if you're in tech and need design that actually respects the complexity of your product, lowercase is frankly unmatched.

HANNAH AHN

@ superpower

we explored a couple of design partners before finding lowercase, and nothing quite hit the mark like they did. their creative approach is just different - in the best way possible. instead of recycling design trends, they design solutions that actually felt like us.

BEN BURKE

@ krazam

we’ve learned to trust their aesthetic taste completely.

AIDEN ROBERTS

wasn't even a core goal but hubspot conversion percentages are up 300% since we launched the website, has paid for itself in pipeline within a week.

ANNIE LIAO

you guys are amazing ❤️ just saw the site it looks lit, ahhhh u guys smashed this!!

SAM ZHENG

they deliver excellent design and they are fun to work with.

ALEX VALENTE

@ redactive

these guys are an essential part of our arsenal. been working with them for a long time now and they've basically become a part of our team. having engineering chops means they grasp our complex tech almost instantly, and they've never once missed a deadline.

DAN FARAHANI

@ bookclub

they moved so fast we were usually the ones blocking them. craft, quality and communication are all fantastic.

JENNY WANG

@ alta

our experience with the team was fantastic. they were super quick in getting things done and really thoughtful with their recommendations—always ready with both long-term strategies and quick fixes. communication was a breeze, whether we were jumping into huddles or catching up through their screen recordings. working with them felt effortless, and their proactive approach made a big difference.

SHIVA KILARU

@ krazam

these guys studied our vibes like a textbook, and nailed down who we were so authentically. which if you know our audience, is exceptionally hard to do. the new website instantly resonated with our fans, and we've received so much hype because of it.

LUKE LANGFORD

@ userflux

especially loved how these guys really understood what we were trying to achieve from the start. they translated our vision into something that genuinely represents our brand in the market.

hills we'll die on
FORTUNE FAVOURS THE FEARLESS. the willingness to try new things, experiment and not conform will always end in a better results for everyone.
ALWAYS DELIVER ON WHAT WAS PROMISED. when people believe in us, we play a part in shaping their tomorrows. trust is currency.
FLOW BUILDS FORCE. in the wave of momentum, each step naturally pulls toward the next. this is what helps keep the buzz for all parties.
QUALITY WHISPERS IN THE DETAILS. excellence is made up of upholding our standards even when it might not be noticed by others.
INTENT GUIDES EVERY DECISION. every line of code, every pixel designed. everything here has earned its place. nothing exists without reason.

About Manish

Hi! I’m Manish, a designer from India. I grew up in a place of extremes, where summers and winters shape how you endure and adapt.




Right now, I’m working on an AI-powered productivity tool exploring how people think and create alongside intelligent systems. I’ve worked across digital products, brands, and physical design, moving between disciplines and figuring things out as I go.




I enjoy being in spaces where things are still undefined, where design meets code and intuition shapes structure. My approach is hands on, experimental, and always evolving.




In my spare time, I’m usually experimenting and building small things, always learning about new areas like robotics, aeronautics, and software, following curiosity wherever it leads.

Get in touch

Find me on X, GitHub, or on Earth. You can also email me for work, opportunities, or conversations around AI, product design, and building things from scratch.

Built to move

Like the horse, I work best in motion. With the teams I work with, I find the clear way through and build the tools that get us there. Here's how that crossing works.

Small talk

The short ones are here. For anything else, ask the cloud.

How did you get into design?

I've loved sci-fi and tech since I was a kid, and my favourite game was Minecraft. That's where I learned to think in systems: a few simple blocks, and rules you can build anything from.

At 17 I wanted to build my own, so I tried to learn Swift from a tutorial. The app it built was pastel shapes with drop shadows, and I couldn't stand it, so I redesigned it before I'd finished learning the code. Looking for how an interface should look, I found a design community online that didn't know my name. I felt part of it anyway, and I stayed.

What's your main thing?

Design first, then the system underneath, in code. I make founders' products easy to get, so customers buy and investors say yes.

Honestly, I'm more of a people person than a design person. Design is the best excuse I've found to get what's in someone's head out where everyone can see it, and then argue about the spacing.

Where are you based?

Currently based in Seoul 
. Before that, five years in The Hague in the Netherlands, and originally from a small village in Poland.

Where do you see yourself in the future?

Somewhere fast and lively, San Francisco could be great, at a startup I believe in, with a GOATed team. Getting as good at the craft as I can, and building the community with designers in my spare time: events, dinners and some fun hangouts.

Outside the 12-hour workdays, some time for art, and of course lots of running ;)

How can I get in touch?

Book a call from the bar, or email andreaskruszakin@gmail.com. Tell me what you're building and where it's hard to get. I write back.

And if your question isn't up here, ask the cloud. I hate talking about myself, so I taught it to do that for me.

Inbox v12, 390

Overview

How might we keep every iteration, and the reason behind it, without slowing down?
Context

This year I moved my whole process from Figma into code. An AI agent in Cursor writes most of it, and Cheval, the design system I build my products on, is the source of truth. In late September I started a folder of prototypes next to Cheval, to see the work, compare it and hand it off in one place. It grew into Cheval Studio, the tool I design every page in, this portfolio included.

Problem

Moving into code fixed the handoff and lost the trail. Every AI tool I tried, Cursor, v0, Lovable and Figma Make, edits a design inside a chat, one change on top of the last. What I tried, and why I dropped it, lives in that chat's context, and the next chat starts without it. So my iterations, and the reasons behind them, got lost.

Fast to try
Real to ship
Make me an inbox
Send
A single AI tool
Fast, but it doesn't know the product, so the screen gets redrawn before anyone can build it.
The sweet spot
A
A v2
A v3
Cheval Studio
Fast, and every screen is the product's own, so a pick hands off as a diff.
Build
6 min
Review
1 day
Tests
412
The product codebase
Real, but every idea pays for the build, the review and the test suite.

Competitor analysis

Six tools, and each one stops at the same wall

I gave the tools people kept recommending the same brief: three directions for one landing section, in the product's own design system. None kept the directions side by side in the real code.

Figma Make
Prototypes inside Figma, but redraws the library instead of using it.
v0
Fast drafts in real React, but every idea is its own chat.
Lovable
A whole app from a few sentences, and only one version of it.
Cursor
Changes the real codebase, but the iterations live in chat history.
Paper
A canvas agents can read and write, kept apart from the product's repo.
Subframe
Hands over clean React, built on its own components instead of the product's.

Then the kits closest to what the studio does. DialKit tunes a component's values live, and the studio's Dials runs on it. Agentation pins notes on elements for an agent. Each covers one need well. None keeps the iterations.

Product
	Tune values live	Notes for the agent	Variants side by side	Every version kept	The product's own system	Works for a team

Cheval Studio
All six, in the product's own repo.
	
	
	
	
	
	


DialKit
Live control panels for a component's values.
	
					

Agentation
Click an element, write a note, hand it to the agent.
		
				

Storybook
Components in isolation, with controls and docs.
					
	


Figma Make
Prompt to prototype, inside Figma.
			
			


v0
Prompt to React, one chat per idea.
						

Cursor
An agent in the real codebase.
					
	
Covers the need
Covers some of it
Doesn't cover it

Research

Prototyping was fine. Keeping track was the problem.

I talked to eight designers from my circle, about half an hour each, and read eight Reddit threads and the public reviews of the tools above. Every note went on one FigJam board and got sorted until the piles stopped moving.

Interview guide, semi-structured
Walk me through the last thing you designed, from the first sketch to what got built.
Where do you prototype now, and what made you pick it?
When you try several directions, where do they live, and how do you compare them?
Tell me about a time a detail got lost between your design and the build.
How do you show a prototype to someone else, and what do they send back?
Have you tried an AI design or coding tool? When did you stop trusting it?
If you could keep one thing from every iteration, what would it be?

Two piles were about the code: it never matches, and the AI tools don't use the system. The other three were about keeping track: comparing directions, remembering why, and showing someone else. Nobody I spoke to had a tool for that second half.

Solution

A studio that runs the product's design system, so a prototype hands off as a diff
Every iteration is kept

Feedback on a variant becomes its next version, set beside the one before it. The live page is the latest version, and the older ones still render.

Iterations

Some things that I removed

Most of what I added stayed. Three things didn't. Each one worked, and each one cost the studio something it needed more.

Taken out
Interface sound
Every card and click played a sound, with a speaker in the sidebar to turn it off. Two days later I took it out. A tool I sit in all day should be quiet.

Agentation for notes
Edit started as Agentation, which waits for a second click on its own toolbar. The studio's own picker starts on the first one.
Taken out
A second table of contents
The guide pages came with a reading rail that repeated the sidebar's links. It's gone from the studio and kept for case studies like this one.

Teamwork

Everyone works in their own folder, and the history knows whose change it was

Each person has a folder in the repo, and every prototype and tool in it is theirs. The studio reads who made what from the folder a commit touched, so a teammate's work is credited without anyone filling in a form.

About

I help founders turn rough ideas into clean, fast products that convert — designed and built end to end.

An Engineer who designs and a Designer who builds. I started freelancing in 2021 and have since partnered with 35+ founders, product teams, and startups — shipping SaaS products, landing pages, dashboards, and design systems that are used daily by real users.

My background spans both sides of the stack: Figma for design systems and interactive prototypes, React and TypeScript in Next.js for implementation, deployed on Vercel. I design the interface and write the code that ships it — so nothing gets lost in handoff. Most design-to-engineering handoffs bleed time and fidelity. My workflow: start in Figma to define the interaction model and visual system, then move directly into implementation with React, TypeScript, and Tailwind. I think in components — both design components and code components — so the hand-off from one to the other is seamless.

Things I believe in

Everyone is fighting a battle they rarely talk about.

Love people while they're still here.

The older I get, the more I realize life is less about finding yourself and more about choosing who you become.

Peace is expensive. It costs ego, comparison, and the need to be understood.

The people you become jealous of are often just mirrors of the life you haven't committed to yet.

Time doesn't heal everything. It teaches you how to carry what never left.

Most regrets aren't about failure. They're about hesitation.

You don't become fearless. You simply decide that something matters more than your fear.

The days feel long. The years disappear.

Nothing changes overnight. Everything changes over years.

One day you'll realize that ordinary moments were the ones you were going to miss the most.

SEED STAGE TO NASDAQ-LISTED CLIENTS

A website making BTQ’s quantum security tangible for a public-market audience

BTQ is a public company securing critical infrastructure against quantum threats. The challenge was to communicate its work to investors and potential partners without losing them in technical complexity.

New immersive 3D website gives an abstract subject a tangible visual form. The experience gives BTQ a better way to present its technology and the scale of its ambitions.

An investor-ready brand and website for PayPath’s Series A ambitions

PayPath now has a stronger presence for fund raising conversations, with a brand that reflects its ambition to modernize debt software. 

Already backed by a16z, the company needed to make its next chapter compelling to investors. A distinctive identity and interactive website sets it apart from legacy providers, while also making the platform easier to understand.

Bynario’s edge is finding exploitable vulnerabilities other tools miss. Its new website brings that difference to the surface, taking visitors inside the binaries where those vulnerabilities live. 

The experience gives prospective customers a distinctive introduction to its approach. Technical depth becomes something visitors can explore through a visual concept rooted in the product itself.

Concourse gives finance teams at companies like Palo Alto Networks AI agents that handle real financial work. Its new website makes that offering easier to evaluate before a sales conversation. 

Enterprise buyers get a clearer picture of how the platform fits their workflows, with complex capabilities explained through motion and custom UI illustrations.

With 50,000+ readers, The Signal needed an identity that matched its growing presence in AI media.

PAX now has a brand that reflects the responsibility of recovering import duties for companies like Glossier, Yamaha, and Verkada.

Bridging software and industry through Axilon’s web presence

Axilon’s website gives software buyers and plant-floor operators a shared understanding of how its technology helps prevent industrial failures. 

Each audience needed a different way into the same product: a clear software proposition for buyers and practical relevance for operators. The design brings both perspectives together, connecting the platform’s capabilities to the industrial environments it serves.

Giving Cluster a new identity in the complex world of AI agents

Cluster’s brand and website give potential customers a clear picture of what their agents can do with the right infrastructure. The platform connects 50+ GTM data sources, LinkedIn and email outreach, and hundreds of coordinated subagents. 

A distinctive identity and custom illustrations bring that system to life, showing how agents work together to execute real go-to-market plays.

Turning early interest in Enroute Health into launch-day demand

Enroute Health built a growing waitlist ahead of launch, with a brand and website that gave people a clear reason to sign up. Its focus on health and athletic performance shaped the experience, connecting the lab’s offering to its audience’s ambitions. 

A visual identity grounded in sport, precision, and science helped establish credibility from the first visit.

Introducing Daena’s vision for enterprise AI that stays entirely yours

Daena’s brand and website gave its private AI offering a clear, cohesive presence, bringing three connected products into one story.

What does your process look like?

We start by defining scope, goals, and constraints. Then I move straight into design, share progress early, iterate quickly, and ship. No long workshops, no unnecessary steps. We communicate through Slack or Telegram.

What happens after I submit the form?

I review your request and get back to you within a few days. If it’s a good fit, we jump on a short call to confirm scope, timeline, and budget. After that, I send a proposal and we can start.

Do you offer Framer development only?

Yes. At the moment, I focus exclusively on Framer development. I collaborate with Kamil, a Framer Pro Experts. This allows me to deliver production-ready builds with highest quality, speed, and zero friction during handoff.

Do you work solo or with a team?

I lead every project myself. When needed, I collaborate with a small group of trusted designers and developers. You always deal directly with me.

How long do projects usually take?

Most projects take 4–8 weeks, depending on scope. Smaller websites move fast. More complex or highly custom work takes longer. Timelines are agreed upfront.

Something ambitious in mind?   Let’s give it the design it deserves.

I've cared about how things look and work for as long as I can remember. That eventually became a design studio, building websites and brands mostly for tech and AI companies because that's the world I find most interesting.

In my free time, I make AI art for myself, and write about design on x.com, where about 25k people stick around. Some of my best client relationships started there.

I do the work myself. That hasn't changed, and I don't plan on it changing.

What does your process look like?

We start by defining scope, goals, and constraints. Then I move straight into design, share progress early, iterate quickly, and ship. No long workshops, no unnecessary steps. We communicate through Slack or Telegram.

What happens after I submit the form?

I review your request and get back to you within a few days. If it’s a good fit, we jump on a short call to confirm scope, timeline, and budget. After that, I send a proposal and we can start.

Do you offer Framer development only?

Yes. At the moment, I focus exclusively on Framer development. I collaborate with Kamil, a Framer Pro Experts. This allows me to deliver production-ready builds with highest quality, speed, and zero friction during handoff.

Do you work solo or with a team?

I lead every project myself. When needed, I collaborate with a small group of trusted designers and developers. You always deal directly with me.

How long do projects usually take?

Most projects take 4–8 weeks, depending on scope. Smaller websites move fast. More complex or highly custom work takes longer. Timelines are agreed upfront.

Manifesto
Teams ship fast early, then hit a wall where design decisions start affecting growth, sales, and investor confidence.

Founders move fast, ship features, and postpone design leadership. Then growth slows, conversion leaks appear, and suddenly design is holding back fundraising, sales, and product clarity.

At that point, execution isn't the problem. Direction is.

JBW exists to bring design leadership in, before it becomes a blocker

We work as an extension of your team — aligning design with business goals and focusing on outcomes that matter: adoption, conversion, and investor confidence.

Matt Sellers — Software designer and interface alchemist at Lovable

LFSGD is my creative alias on the internet, born out of the golden age of interface design (aka the Photoshop era).




With over twenty years of experience spent at ~12800% zoom, I've collaborated with some of the world's top studios, innovative startups, and leading companies, offering a blend of craftsmanship and expertise.




At my core is a deep passion obsession for simplicity, meticulous pixel perfection, and human-centric design. 




I specialize in building robust design systems, quality user interfaces, and custom iconography.




Life is good. Let’s create something beautiful together.
