SleekSign

SleekSign is a document-signing workspace. Place fields on a PDF, assign signer roles, share packet links, and collect signatures with audit trails.

SIGNATURE
SIGNING
PDFSIGNING
DOCS
DOC
View project
SleekSign product preview
Problem

In my workplace, the HR wanted every one to sign some document so they sent the document to everybody. However, you needed to find a way to sign the doc, i.e find an e-document app, sign it, & then send it back. People complained because that was a tedius and uncomfortable way to do that. Thus, I decided to simplify & solve this problem. I built SleekSign as the solution.

Building SleekSign, I realized that the visible act of signing a document is only a small part of the real problem. Dragging a signature onto a PDF is straightforward. The difficult work is everything around it: assigning the right fields to the right people, distributing the correct signing links, preserving an audit trail, finalizing one authoritative document, and later proving that the file has not changed.

A signature should be part of a verifiable workflow, not decoration placed on a PDF.

Building the signing workflow

SleekSign is a document-signing workspace. A sender uploads a PDF, places signature, text, date, and checkbox fields, assigns them to signer roles, and shares individual or group links. Signers can type, draw, or upload a signature. The product supports collaborative packets, individual copies, shared-base workflows, CSV bulk sends, reminders, and a grouped audit timeline.

SleekSign Dashboard

The editor forced me to think spatially. PDF coordinates, browser coordinates, zoom levels, page rotations, and responsive layouts all have to agree or a field will land somewhere different from where the sender placed it. That made the editor as much an engineering problem as a design problem.

Making finalization mean something

Building SleekSign, I extended the platform for 3 types of signature packets:

Collaborative packet (Everyone signs the same live document): HR, employee, and witness work on one packet, so each completed signature becomes visible inside the same shared agreement.

Shared-base copies (Company signs once, recipients countersign their own copy): This means that the employer or HR signature is shared across every recipient copy, while each employee or contractor only sees their own private signing section.

Individual copies (One template, separate copies for each signer): This means, every recipient signs their own copy, so nobody sees anyone else’s signature, date, or private form data. This is the basic and exactly the problem scenario that led me to build SleekSign.

3 Packet models

I later pushed the project beyond collecting marks on a page. When a packet is finalized, SleekSign hashes the PDF, seals the audit chain, creates a canonical verification manifest, and asks Google Cloud KMS to sign its digest with ECDSA P-256/SHA-256. This was also the first time I learned about KMS (considered AWS initially but went with Google because I didnt want to create an AWS account just for it when I'm already using Google for auth).

The resulting receipt records the exact KMS key version used. A public verification flow can then hash an uploaded PDF, rebuild the manifest and audit-chain root, retrieve the public key, and verify the signature locally. If the PDF changes by one byte, verification fails.

The production application reaches KMS through Vercel OIDC and Google Workload Identity Federation, so there is no long-lived service-account JSON key stored in the deployment. There is also no unsigned fallback: if signing, storage, or audit validation fails, finalization fails.

Stack: The application uses 
SvelteKit
, 
TypeScript
, and 
Tailwind CSS
. PDF.js renders documents, pdf-lib creates finalized files, and signature_pad captures drawn signatures. 
PostgreSQL
 and 
Drizzle ORM
 store workflow state, S3-compatible object storage holds documents, 
Resend
 delivers signing links, and 
Google Cloud KMS
 protects the signing key.

What I learned

SleekSign taught me to separate what a product can prove from what its interface implies. The system can prove that a particular PDF matches a receipt signed by SleekSign's protected key and that its stored audit chain is intact. That does not automatically prove every signer's real-world identity, and it is not a replacement for a regulated certificate authority.

That boundary matters. Trust grows when the product is precise about its guarantees, fails clearly, and preserves enough evidence for someone else to verify the result.

Chikọta

A bookmark workspace for capturing, organizing, and finding links, with reminders to revisit saved content and a browser extension for quick capture.

BOOKMARKS
PRODUCTIVITY
SVELTEKIT
View project
Chikọta product preview

We all save things we think we'll need later.

Tweets on X, articles in browser bookmarks, links buried inside bookmark folders, and tabs we refuse to close because they might be important someday.

The problem is that these things eventually end up scattered everywhere.

I use multiple browsers and, over time, my bookmarks grew across all of them. I also had the habit of leaving important tabs open instead of bookmarking them because I knew there was a good chance I'd forget about the bookmark entirely. I love Arc browser and have been using it as my default browser for over a year, but one thing that frustrated me was how inactive tabs would eventually close & get archived. Whenever that happened, I'd have to dig through my history trying to remember what I had open.

I had also come across browser extensions built specifically for bookmarking, but the few ones I checked out, I found they stored bookmarks locally in the browser. That doesn't solve the problem for me. If my bookmarks live in that browser's local storage, then I still need that particular browser and potentially that particular device to access them. Thus, that defeats the entire purpose of what I wanted:

Save something once, then access it anytime, anywhere, and from any device.

Building Chikọta
Chikọta

Early this year, I built a simple version of this solution for myself. The idea was deliberately straightforward: whenever I found something I wanted to keep, instead of bookmarking it on X, leaving a tab open, or adding it to yet another browser folder, I'd paste the link into Chikọta. Then I could find it later from any device.

Chikọta is an Igbo word meaning "to gather."

The name fits what I was building — a single place to gather all the things on the internet I wanted to come back to.

Chikọta about me modal
Bookmarks shouldn't just sit there

While using the first version, I realized another problem with bookmarks: Sometimes, simply saving something isn't enough. There are links I save because I genuinely need to act on them later — this could be an article I want to read, a tool I want to try, documentation I need for a project, or something I need to revisit on a particular day.

So I added reminders.

A bookmark can have a reminder attached to it, and Chikọta can notify me through a device notification or email when it's time to revisit it.

Search modal

This changed the product slightly in my head. Chikọta wasn't just becoming a place to store links. It was becoming a place to remember why I saved them in the first place.

Search modal brown theme
Rethinking the experience

A few months later, I returned to the project.

The first version worked, but it was very obviously something I had built to solve a problem quickly. I wanted to explore what the product could feel like if I treated the experience and visual design with the same level of attention as the functionality. After all, I'm a Frontend Engineer. Even a private tool I use myself deserves to feel considered.

I looked at a few interfaces and websites, specifically EchoTab, I liked the design choice and I used those as references while designing a second version.

But the redesign wasn't only visual.

I also started thinking about where the act of bookmarking actually happens. Usually, I'm already inside a browser when I discover something worth saving. Opening another website, copying a URL, navigating to Chikọta, and pasting it introduces unnecessary friction. So V2 extends Chikọta outside of the main application.

There’s now a browser extension that lets me right-click a page or link and save it to Chikọta. It opens the app in a new tab and adds the link automatically. The extension is simply a way in; when I’m signed in, the bookmark lives in my Chikọta account and is available across devices.

I also added a desktop widget for quickly accessing bookmarks without needing to open the browser at all. The goal was to make Chikọta less like a destination I had to remember to visit and more like a small utility that was available whenever I needed it.

Version 2
Current Chikota Dashboard
Engineering Chikọta

Stack: Chikọta uses 
SvelteKit
, 
TypeScript
, and 
Tailwind CSS
 for the interface. 
Drizzle ORM
 and 
PostgreSQL
 persist the bookmark library and its relationships.

A few decisions shaped how Chikọta works across these different surfaces:

The browser extension is an entry point, not another bookmark store. Right-clicking a page or link opens Chikọta with its details ready to save automatically. I also added a small prompt when a URL is copied. Both flows lead back to the same account-based collection rather than storing bookmarks inside the browser.

The desktop experiences follow the conventions of their platforms. WidgetKit on macOS works within fixed sizes and intentionally limits interaction, so anything requiring text input opens the companion app. On Linux, I use a resizable desktop window instead, which allows bookmarks to be added, searched, and organized directly.

Desktop access has its own authentication flow. The desktop apps use an account-issued token to communicate with the same bookmark API as the web application, without relying on an active browser session.

Saved links remain useful offline. Each desktop app keeps a local copy of the last synchronized collection, so bookmarks can still be browsed and opened when there is no internet connection.

What I learned

Building Chikọta reinforced something I've increasingly come to believe about product design:

The best interface isn't always another interface.

The first version solved the storage problem, but it still required me to adapt my behavior around the product. The browser extension, reminders, and desktop widget came from asking a different question: How can the product adapt to the way I already behave? It also reinforced the difference between making a feature convenient and making the underlying system genuinely accessible.

A browser extension alone wasn't enough. If the data remained trapped inside that browser, I would just be creating another bookmark silo. The extension needed to be an input mechanism, not the database. That distinction shaped one of the core ideas behind Chikọta: the experience can exist across browsers and devices, while the user's collection remains unified. It also became an exercise in balancing engineering and design.

I wasn't designing an interface first and then figuring out how to implement it, nor was I building functionality and adding polish afterward. The product evolved through both at the same time; interaction decisions affected the technical architecture, and technical possibilities shaped the experience.

Chikọta started as a tiny utility I built because I was tired of losing things on the internet. It eventually became an exploration of how something as ordinary as bookmarking could be made calmer, more accessible, and more intentional.

A workbench that connects what you select in the browser to the source that made it.

Atelier keeps interface changes grounded in the repository. Select something in the rendered page, inspect the source and relationships behind it, make a direct change or ask for a focused proposal, then review the diff and checks before deciding what stays.

Next.js
TypeScript
Graphify
Groq
Git
PROBLEM

Visual editing becomes hard to trust when the rendered element, its source, and the resulting code change are treated as separate things. A quick tweak can lose context, touch the wrong file, or become difficult to review.

SELECTION TO SOURCE

Atelier maps a rendered selection back to its owning file and source location. The selection narrows the task; Graphify-style relationships add only the surrounding files needed to understand it.

BOUNDED PROPOSALS

Direct controls and model proposals pass through the same allowlist and exact-source checks. A proposal can change only the supplied paths and text, and a fresh read refuses to overwrite work that changed outside Atelier.

REVIEW AND RECOVERY

Every accepted change updates the preview and remains visible as a diff. Checks, undo, redo, and Revert changes make experimentation reviewable and give the interface a clear way back.

TWO MODES

The hosted demo uses a bundled Sunday Studio fixture and keeps edits, history, and a tester-supplied Groq key in the current tab only. Explicit local mode works with trusted projects and adds persistent workspaces, real project checks, branches, commits, push, and pull request publication.

BOUNDARY

The demo does not execute arbitrary generated code or expose local Git operations. Refreshing restores the clean fixture. Local mode keeps the broader workflow behind explicit configuration and user actions.

observations.text:

Multiply

Summer 2026

withmultiply.com
04Reflections
— show all sections
00
Context
Role
Design Intern
Team
PM, Engineering Team, & one other designer
Skills
Design, UI/UX, Prototyping
What is Multiply?

Multiply helps employers offer financial benefits, with mortgages at the center of the product during my internship. Borrowers discover Multiply through their employer, apply for a mortgage, and work with our internal loan officers to complete their loan. As the first design intern, I focused on making that process easier for the people helping them through it.

Goal

Make getting a mortgage smoother for both the person applying and the loan officer helping them through the process.

Helping loan officers know what to do next.

Over the summer, I redesigned Multiply’s internal command center and CRM, working on the tools our loan officers used to manage loans and stay in touch with borrowers. I wanted someone logging in to know what needed their attention and how to get it done.

A main project, and a little bit of everything

I owned the product design for the CRM and command center. Our PM helped set direction, engineering built the designs, and the other designer gave feedback while focusing primarily on our rebrand and marketing work. I worked within an existing design system, but had room to establish new interactions and navigation patterns.

I really enjoyed having one project I could go deep on while also working on whatever came up along the way. If a loan officer got stuck, something needed fixing, or product wanted to add a feature, I got to jump in.

01
A command center
that grew up

The command center had grown organically. New tools kept getting added, but the navigation was still built around one or two use cases. Each tool had its own layout, and the experience felt fragmented.

There wasn’t really a dashboard yet, only a starting point with links to different tools. As the product grew, helping loan officers find a feature was only part of the problem. We also needed to help them figure out what to do when they got there.

Before · a list of tools

The original starting point asked loan officers what they wanted to do, but offered little context about what needed attention.
Understanding how people actually worked

I watched dozens of session replays, looked at usage metrics, and talked individually with loan officers. I first met with them to understand the problems they were running into, then came back with variations and potential directions.

This was especially useful because what a loan officer wanted to do wasn’t always the same as what product wanted to encourage. I had to understand both: make the tool useful in their day-to-day work, while helping drive outcomes like more consistent borrower outreach.

Finding a structure the product could grow into

I explored top navigation, sidebars, and combinations of the two. A lot of the work was figuring out a layout and framework that could bring the tools together and still give us room to move things around as the product changed.

I landed on a mix of top navigation and a sidebar. The sidebar gave the different tools a consistent home, so moving between prospects, applications, and loans felt like working within one product.

Exploration · bringing the tools together

Different approaches to navigation, explored around the same loan management workflow.
From a starting page to a plan for the day

The dashboard became a place to see actionable tasks, borrowers who needed attention, and the status of active loans. Each section connected to the relevant tool or next action.

Working with product and the loan officers helped determine what belonged here. One example was surfacing a borrower who hadn’t been contacted in the past week. That gave the officer a reason to reach out and helped keep people from falling through the cracks.

After · a clearer next step

Tasks, outreach, and loan status give the day a starting point.

On mobile

The mobile layout brings tools and tasks into a narrower view.
Shipping, listening, and going back in

I presented the redesign at Integral, our weekly company-wide all hands, and kept iterating after feedback. One small change was adding names on hover to the collapsed sidebar. With the sidebar open, the labels were obvious; when it collapsed, the icons had to do all the work. The hover labels made it possible to check what each icon meant.

The entire dashboard and navigation redesign shipped, and I had time to keep refining it. Getting to see the work used—and then improve it—was one of the most valuable parts of the summer.

One navigation across tools

The shared sidebar carries through to the prospect list.

Sidebar collapsed

Collapsed, the icons carry the navigation, and hovering one shows its name.
A second view for loans in progress

One smaller project came out of processing. Loans there lived on a kanban board, which showed where each loan was but not what it was waiting on. Loan officers and processors had to open a loan to find out whether the appraisal was back or the rate lock had expired.

I added a list view alongside the board. It keeps the same stages, but gives each loan a row of statuses: rate lock, title, appraisal, insurance, HOA, and the initial closing disclosure. Each one is colored like a traffic light, and funding dates are flagged when they slip. Both views shipped, with a toggle to switch between them.

Cards · where each loan is

The board shows each loan’s stage and how long it has been there.

List · what each loan still needs

The list puts every outstanding item on one row, with problems in red.
02
A shared picture
of each borrower

Multiply already had a basic CRM, but it was fragmented and difficult to use. Notes and marketing emails were there, while conversations between loan officers and borrowers lived in individual inboxes. Usage data also showed gaps: activity wasn’t being logged, and many borrower records had little activity.

This mattered because one borrower could be supported by a team of loan officers, and branch managers sometimes needed to check in too. An individual inbox couldn’t give everyone the same picture of what was happening.

Bringing the conversation into the CRM

I redesigned the activity log and cleaned up the surrounding experience, bringing loan officer and borrower emails alongside notes and marketing emails. The goal was to give the team one place to understand the relationship and pick up where someone else left off.

Before · the existing activity log

The original CRM provided a basic place to record contact and notes.

After · more context in one place

A fuller activity history sits alongside borrower information and a place to add a new entry.

Within a loan

The activity log brings different types of communication into one history.

On mobile

The same history, adapted to a smaller screen.

4×

More contacts with leads

One of the results I’m most proud of was seeing four times as many contacts with leads following the dashboard, navigation, and CRM improvements. The changes made it easier for loan officers to see who needed attention and work through their outreach.

126 → 427

Notes logged per week, on average, after the activity log and note-taking changes.

Under 50% → ~95%

Contacted by a loan officer within 24 hours of signing up or asking a question.

Leads contacted within 24 hours, by week. The rate climbed as changes to the dashboard, activity log, and note-taking shipped through May, and it has stayed between 80% and 100% every week since June.

Just as meaningful was hearing directly from the people using it. Paul, one of our loan officers, described how the redesign helped the team manage its pipeline and stay on top of outreach.

“This redesign made navigation extremely smooth, allowing our sales team to manage its pipeline and really dial-in our client outreach cadence and tracking.”

Paul Gresh
Loan officer, Multiply
03
A detour into emails

While working on the product, I took a short break to redesign our emails. We were switching to a more modern email platform during the rebrand, which meant rebuilding emails, workflows, and customer journeys.

I owned the email redesign and came up with several new designs. Then we had another problem: there were dozens of individual emails to implement in code.

Making the next email easier to build

I worked with the marketing team to develop reusable email components and implemented them in code. Then I created a custom Claude skill with instructions for our design system, the components, and how to use them together.

The marketing team could use a simple prompt or a screenshot of a design to create a new email. That gave them a way to keep building with the system after the initial redesign.

Before · text under a logo

Earlier emails were mostly plain text with a single button.

After · built from shared components

A welcome email for employer partners, assembled from the new components.

“Sam built a custom Claude skill that cut the project timeline from several months down to just a few weeks.”

Madison
Marketing, Multiply
04
What I’m taking
with me
Designing with the people using it

Being able to talk directly with loan officers, watch how they worked, and come back with something new made the process feel immediate. I got to move quickly, but also go deep. Almost everything I worked on shipped, and hearing that people loved the new experience meant a lot to me.

Learning to hand off, and stay involved

This was my first time working with a full engineering team instead of developing my own designs. I learned to communicate through more detailed Figma wireframes and prototypes, and to think through the states and interactions someone else would need to build.

Having experience building products helped a lot: I could speak the engineers’ language and jump into the codebase during QA to help get the details right. Handoff became another part of the collaboration.

New doesn’t always mean most important

One lesson that stuck with me was recency bias in design. When we’re working on a new feature, it’s easy to want to make it the most visible thing in the product. But stepping back and looking at the whole experience, that isn’t always the right decision. Designing the command center made me think more carefully about where a feature belongs in someone’s actual workflow.

I came away really enjoying this kind of work: owning something substantial, staying close to the people using it, and getting to help with the smaller things that make the whole product better.

With the Multiply team at our San Francisco office.
Building products that
people care about

I love designing products and the stories behind
them. I’d love to connect on LinkedIn, X (Twitter),
or Instagram. If you’d like to reach out, you can also
send me an email at sam@samfcheng.com.

Why me?

I design products that work. Most of what I build gets approved on the first pass—95% acceptance rate—because I'm focused on solving the actual problem, not dressing it up. Clean interfaces, clear thinking, no BS!

How I work

Stage 1

Structure first

I start with wireframes to define user flow, hierarchy, and key decisions so the product structure is right before visuals are introduced.

Stage 2

Design & prototype

I translate the structure into high fidelity designs and interactive prototypes that reflect the real product experience.

Stage 3

Document & handoff

I finalize designs with clear documentation and specs to ensure smooth handoff and accurate implementation.

My story

About

I believe good design is quiet. It doesn’t shout it guides, invites, and feels natural. Through every layout and interaction, I seek balance between precision and personality.

About

My path into design began with an interest in how things work — and evolved into how things feel. Now, I design experiences that merge usability with emotion, ensuring that every pixel has purpose. My process revolves around curiosity, structure, and restraint, turning complexity into clarity through thoughtful detail. Each project is an exploration of balance between function and feeling, precision and simplicity.

About

Design, for me, is less about decoration and more about direction. It’s about guiding people, simplifying choices, and turning uncertainty into flow. That’s the mindset I bring to every project I work on.

Maximilian Inzinger,

is a brand designer and design engineer based in Copenhagen. With a background in type design, he brings an attention to language, form and rhythm to the work – from the pace of a publication to the way a website moves and responds. Working independently through Office of Personal Responsibility and with studios including Bielke&Yang, Alexis Mark, Other Means, Approximate Type and Studio Malpeso, he has developed typefaces, identities, books and websites for clients including Netflix, the Guston Foundation, Aarhus School of Architecture, Rigshospitalet, MuseumsQuartier Wien, Nikolaj Kunsthal and the Heidi Horten Collection. A graduate and teaching assistant at ÉCAL’s Master Type Design programme, he has also given guest lectures and workshops at Pratt Institute in New York and VERA skole for kunst & design in Copenhagen. He is building Cicero, a macOS font manager, meantime, a private location journal for iPhone, and other independent software projects.

OVERVIEW

Redesigning and rebuilding Ballogy’s 300K+ user sports app

We’ve partnered with Ballogy for 9+ months to overhaul the full mobile product experience, then moved into a focused 3-month engagement to rebuild the iOS and Android frontend.

Live athlete development platform
300K+ users

"Mobile app looks amazing. Super pleased with the first build. We knew you guys would crush this!"

Jordan Green
COO @Ballogy

What we did

Mobile app design

Marketing assets

CLIENT
Ballogy

Book an intro call
Send email

YEAR
2025-current

Overview
UX rework
Athlete app
Coaches and teams
Parents
Visual system

Website
About the project

Ballogy helps young athletes train, prove it on video, and get seen, recording their reps, tracking progress, and sharing it in one place. We're redesigning the entire app and helping build the 2.0 so it can scale from basketball to every sport.

Ballogy wasn't starting from zero. It already had a live app and a real community of players, coaches, and parents, along with years of features layered on top of each other, an onboarding flow that was losing new users, and a basketball-first experience that now had to stretch across 18 sports. We were brought in to redesign every flow, onboarding, home, feed, training, and profiles, and to lead the build alongside their engineering team.

This case study explains how we got there.

Client
Ballogy
Industry
Sports training & athlete development (mobile app)
Services
App redesign (UX/UI) · Product design · Design system · Frontend and backend development · Website design · Marketing assets
Timeline
2025 - present
Play again
The challenge

Ballogy wasn't a blank slate. It had a working app, real users, and years of accumulated features, which made the rebuild harder, not easier.

The job wasn't to invent a product. It was to take an app that already worked, simplify what had grown complex, and rebuild it to scale, without losing the users, data, and habits people already relied on. It also had to be safe for minors, flexible enough for parents and coaches, and fast, all while multiple teams built at once against a tight clock.

"We had quite a lengthy onboarding process in our existing app, and we saw that people were dropping off, they weren't getting into the app, which is why we shortened it."

Saad Hussain · CTO, Ballogy
01
One structure, three users
Players, coaches, and parents shared similar flows despite having different goals.
02
Growing product complexity
Years of features and real users meant every change had to respect what already worked.
03
Depth that had to stay
Real tracking, coaching, and team tools couldn't be stripped out, only made clearer.
04
Built for basketball, needed every sport
A basketball-first experience had to scale across 18 sports without leaving sections empty.
05
Safe for minors, built for families
Under-13 rules, parent-managed profiles, and coach, player, and parent roles all had to live in one account system.
06
Built to scale
Whatever we shipped had to hold up across roles, sports, and future growth.
Our approach

We approached the rebuild from both sides at once. First off, redesigning the UI to make the whole thing feel premium.

On the UI side, we moved to a premium dark mobile interface with stronger visual hierarchy, consistent components, cleaner cards, tabs, and bottom sheets, bigger and clearer typography, more expressive progress data, and custom badges and achievement moments that give the product personality.

UX rework

And most importantly, untangling the complex user journeys

On the UX side, we built clear role-based journeys, simplified onboarding and profile setup, structured the coach workflows, made progress and performance tracking easier to read.

We also tightened the access, invite, and contact-sharing flows so the app felt safe for every user, including minors.

Solution

One product, three different experiences

Instead of one app bent to fit everyone, we split Ballogy into three purpose-built journeys.

Player to track progress, training, achievements, and team activity. Coach to manage teams, workouts, calendars, communication, and performance. Parent to stay connected to their child's activity, schedule, coach updates, and team messages.

Same platform, three clear front doors.

Players
New athlete experience

We redesigned the athlete experience to feel structured, motivating, and progress-driven, connecting onboarding, training, performance, achievements, and team activity into one clear journey.

A sports identity from the first session.

Onboarding now opens with a sport picker, player details, and a training path, so the app feels personal from the very first screen. Players choose their sport, position, experience level, and weekly commitment, and start earning legacy points before they've even finished setting up.

Demo-first experience

After picking a sport, users can enter the app as a fully clickable demo, prefilled with sample data, metrics, and stats.

The profile is prefilled with sample data, metrics, and statistics, so users can explore real screens, real flows, and real product value before creating a full account, which lowers the barrier that was costing plenty of sign-ups before.

Play again
Play again
Clearer home base

Complex performance data becomes easier to scan

The redesigned home turns complex performance data into something scannable: circular scores, compact stat cards, activity bars, shooting maps, leaderboard positions, and trend charts that make raw numbers actionable at a glance.

Play again
Daily progress tracking

Players activities all come down to a single loop: train, track, understand, get rewarded, come back stronger.

Players act, every action is captured, insights show them what's improving, rewards reinforce the effort, and the system gives them a reason to return.

Play again
Training tools

Smaller tools for the work between sessions.

A calibration setup gets shot tracking ready before a session, from where the tripod stands to a countdown. Focus drills and mindset timers guide breathing and attention, and run sessions turn into stories players can share.

Gamification

Turning progress into something players can feel

Gamified moments like badges, redeemable points, and achievement tiers (the 500 and 10k Shot Club, rewards such as a PRO subscription, a Ballogy tee, or a signed ball) turn activity into real-world rewards and make the app feel alive.

Play again
Badges and rewards
01
Badges
02
Redeem points
Turn player activity into real-world rewards
Coaches
Everything in one place

We brought team setup, training, calendars, communication, player progress, and AI support into one clear structure, organized around five core workflows.

Team performance at a glance

Coaches can see team activity, training, movement, and recovery all at once.

They can now compare individual player progress without opening multiple views, and track completion, overdue workouts, and daily activity, all anchored by Ballogy's MTR performance metric.

Play again
Team coordination

One place to plan, communicate, and keep the team moving.

Calendar to schedule trainings, games, deadlines, and RSVPs. Chats to keep team, parent, and player communication in one place. Feed to switch between global and team-specific updates. Team to manage rosters, performance, workouts, and settings. Profile for account, subscription, and notifications.

An AI coach built in

AI support built into the coaching workflow

We added an AI assistant inside the coaching experience that answers player-development questions and recommends workouts and drills on demand, so a coach can turn "help my players improve footwork" into a ready-to-assign plan in seconds.

Parents
Different purpose entirely

In the old app, parents were basically a copy of the player.

In the new app, we separated it into a dedicated role with a different purpose: visibility, coordination, and support

Parent-child linking

Making parent-child linking understandable

Parent setup solves one specific UX challenge: making it clear whose account is being created, whose profile is being tracked, and how the two connect. Access code first, separate parent details, then child-profile confirmation, so ownership is never ambiguous.

Parent dashboard

A parent dashboard focused on clarity

Parents get progress, training, performance, and highlights in one place: development without digging through screens, completed sessions and recent activity, key metrics like MTR, shooting accuracy, and recovery, and the standout moments worth seeing.

Sharper visual system

None of this scales without a system.

We rebuilt Ballogy's interface to feel darker, more premium, and easier to scan, while staying flexible across player, coach, and parent.

Play again
Launch film concept

An early concept for the launch film.

Storyboards and design in Figma, animated in After Effects. The team went with a different direction in the end, but the character animation was worth showing.

Play again
The website

Ballogy sells three products to three audiences, so the website gives each one its own front door.

We designed ballogy.com
(opens in a new tab)
 in Figma and built it in Framer: a homepage that introduces the platform, a page each for the app, Coach HQ and Camp HQ, pricing for athletes, teams and camps, and a blog. It uses the same dark, premium system as the app, with Ballogy orange for the moments that sell.

Overview

AM Trades is a trading education platform built by Anthony, helping traders learn through free and premium content, live sessions and a private community.

We were brought in to design and build the entire platform from scratch, covering both the product and the public website.

In 8 weeks, we went from an idea to a live, full-stack platform accepting new users. It now has 12,000+ registered users.

Visit platform
Challenge

Education platforms live or die by the move from free to paid.

If the free experience feels empty, users leave. If premium is pushed too hard, they leave anyway.

AM Trades needed a platform that gave new traders real value from day one, while making the benefits of premium clear at the right moments: daily live sessions, Anthony’s private Discord community and premium courses.

Outcome

We designed and developed the full platform end to end.

Account creation, authentication and onboarding lead into a free dashboard with educational content and custom study tools.

Premium sections, locked states and upgrade journeys introduce the extra value as users explore, without constantly interrupting the free experience. We call this the Expansion Model.

Whop connects the platform to the paid product and membership access, and Klaviyo automates email collection and segmentation after onboarding.

A public landing page supports free registration, and a custom admin panel lets Anthony upload content, control what users see and add admins himself.

Anthony was closely involved throughout. We spoke daily and worked through detailed feedback across design and development, and he never had to ask for the same correction twice.

We also made updates in anticipation of growth beyond 100,000 users.

The result is a platform Anthony fully runs on his own, live in 8 weeks.

Gallery
Testimonial
“I came to Kargul Studio with a specific vision and timeline for an educational platform: a complete onboarding flow, secure account creation, a backend email flow, educational content hosting, custom study tools, multiple sections, locked premium states, converting landing pages, connection to a paid product, and an admin panel to control everything.
In about 8–9 weeks, we went from an idea to a live, full-stack platform taking on new users, plus a public landing page built to convert. Design was done in Figma and then built out in development, with every round of feedback refining the features and user experience. I never had to ask for the same correction twice and even small details I pointed out were handled which was very important to me.
The project manager Deniz was a pleasure to work with. We communicated daily and he never made me feel like asking a question or getting on a meeting was an inconvenience. He instead encouraged and initiated it. The rest of the team showed the same through their work being fast, high quality, open to feedback, and honest when something could be done better.
I’ve learned through experience that nothing is more expensive than a project that never delivers to a final product. Kargul Studio is one of the few teams I’d confidently pay for an agreed outcome before work even begins. If you’re a founder with high standards and a specific vision, you need a team that holds itself to the same level. I’ll be continuing to work with them as my platform grows in the future.”
Anthony

AM Trades

observations.title: Vova Pytsiuk
observations.text:
Builder from Vancouver 🇨🇦

Hi, I'm Vova

Software engineer with 7 years of experience and a master’s in CS. Born and raised in 🇺🇦, based in 🇨🇦. Outside of work: snowboarding, concerts and travelling.

📦 Projects
🤖
Vibe Buddy

A desktop robot that shows usage limits for AI coding tools like Claude Code and Codex, and lets you know when they’re working or finished. I started it as a hobby project with Alize. It ranked #6 on Product Hunt’s daily leaderboard.

↗
🕊️
Played in Russia

Public database tracking artists who perform in russia after the invasion of Ukraine. This is a personal project: I enjoy going to concerts and believe in sanctions and boycotts against countries that disregard the international order and invade others. My Reddit post about it reached 100,000 views, and the project was featured in Ukrainian and European media.

↗
🍁
My Days in Canada

iOS app to track physical presence in Canada for citizenship eligibility, log trips, and optionally scan photos for travel dates — all data stays on-device/iCloud.

↗
Show more
projects
+
👔 Work
DeviantArt

2022 - 2026 · Vancouver, Canada

I developed APIs and data pipelines, ran A/B tests, trained and deployed machine learning models, built full-stack apps and worked with OLAP systems. My stack included AWS (CDK, Lambda, S3, Kinesis, SQS, SNS and Step Functions), Grafana, Kubernetes and Next.js.

I guided a junior developer on an A/B testing management project, designing the system’s architecture and supporting their implementation and QA work.

I independently led and built a high-load replacement for the legacy pipeline that processed every image upload and updates to files, descriptions and other content. I also developed image-processing APIs that ran ML models at 5–8 requests per second. I developed and led an internal marketing tool that sent millions of notifications to users each week.

SoftServe/Cisco

2021 - 2022 · Gdansk, Poland

Our team worked on email spam detection for Cisco Talos, Cisco’s threat intelligence team.

I built a cached translation API designed to handle large volumes of email, translating message content to help the system identify spam.

I wrote extensive technical documentation and worked with Python, Kubernetes, PostgreSQL, Redis and email protocols.

GoBoutique

2019 - 2021 · Lviv, Ukraine

I worked closely with traders to turn their market insights and hypotheses into algorithmic trading strategies. This involved collecting, processing and analyzing financial data, then translating trading ideas into code.

I also built chatbots and automated data pipelines using Kubeflow and AWS Step Functions to collect and prepare data for training machine learning models.

My stack included Python, Vue.js, AWS (S3, Lambda, EC2, Fargate, Step Functions), pandas, NumPy and Plotly.

Design for companies moving forward.

Variant-01 is an independent one-man design studio helping ambitious companies turn complex ideas into clear, compelling digital experiences.  




We work across brand, web, product, and motion, partnering closely with teams that care about what they’re building and how the world experiences it. Independent studio. Global clients. Thoughtful work.

From first impression to everyday experience.

We work across the different layers of how a company presents itself, communicates its value, and interacts with its users.

Web

Websites and landing pages that make your product easier to understand, your positioning sharper, and your business easier to choose.

Brand

Visual identities that give companies a distinct point of view and a system they can grow with.

Digital products and interfaces designed around real people, real workflows, and real problems.

Welcome to my corner of the Internet :-)

I’m Kevin, a product designer studying computer science and cognitive science at UC Berkeley. I was drawn to design because it allows me to enhance people’s lives through the way they interact with technology.

I think of myself first and foremost as an artist, even if it’s not my profession. I started off doodling throughout my childhood, which led me to AP Drawing and studio classes here at Berkeley. Picked up other creative crafts along the way, like photography, graphic design, and crocheting.

You might find me hooping with friends, attempting latte art, or playing piano on my roommate’s 76-key.

Feel free to reach out on LinkedIn, X, or by email. I’d love to chat!

Who I am, what I care about, and where to find me.

Who I am

I'm Zaid Mukaddam, a founder and product person from Mumbai, India. I spend most of my time building Scira AI, an agentic research platform, and the rest of it thinking about tools, cities, and how to build a life that feels like mine.

What I care about

I like products that respect your time. Interfaces that get out of the way. Teams that ship before they are ready, and then keep shipping. I'm drawn to problems where the user is trying to think, not just consume.

observations.title: Streak — A social wallet where every token is a community and every trade climbs its board | velora.studio
observations.text:
Go back
Book an intro call
Streak. A wallet where every trade climbs a board, brand to iPhone.

Brand, web app, landing page and iPhone app for Streak, a crypto wallet where each token is a community with a face. Trading earns XP for that community and moves you up its board, every wallet is a Noun, and the mark is a comet: the way every token streaks across the screen.

Brand · Product Design · iOS · Web App · Landing · 2026

Streak, live
Full screen

It's the real app: open a token, trade it and climb its board

A comet with three trails

One round head and three trails behind it, the way every token streaks across the hero. It sits white on a blue tile, lit along the top edge.

Black, white, and blue when something moves

Soft dark cards, white pills for the one thing to do, blue for what you earn. Each token brings its own two colours, used only on its page, its board and its comet.

Trade, then see what it did

Built for a desktop: a sidebar with the same five places as the iPhone, Home, Tokens, Feed, Analyst and XP, and the communities you've joined under them. Each token is the hub for its price, its board and its chat, and a trade ends on the XP you earned and the rank it bought you.

The product, shown working

A bento of live pieces instead of illustrations: the trade sheet, a token's page, its podium, its chat and the analyst, on a fine square grid that fades out around each one.

The same streak in your pocket

The same five tabs: Home, Tokens, Feed, Analyst and XP. Trades end on the same result panel, and quests send you straight to where you can finish them.

Eight communities, one wallet, and a reason to come back every morning.

Kept
Clients, sessions and payments for freelancers, kept in one calendar

craft is the new moat for your company

For most of software’s history, the hard part was building. If you could ship it, you had an edge.

That has changed quietly over the last few years. With AI, most teams can build a working product in weeks. Ask a model for a settings page and you get the one it has seen most often: it works, and it looks like everyone else’s.

What pulls a product away from that middle is taste, and most of it has reasons you can name. A menu opens fast because people open it fifty times a day. An error says what to do next. An agent’s action can be seen and undone. None of this appears on a feature list, but it is most of what makes people trust a product.

Taste also does not scale by itself. So we write it down early, as foundations: the primitives, the components, how the product speaks and behaves, kept as rules your team and its agents build with.

That is the work we do at Ace. I have spent over 12 years designing products with founders, at companies like ClickUp, Langdock, Twin and Instantly, and I lead every project. We set the foundations with you, design to them blocks by blocks, screen by screen, and stay until the quality holds on its own.

Rico Oktananda

Principal Designer @
Ace

at a time. Sales, marketing, hospitality,

Shaun Latip — Senior Product Designer & Design Engineer

Senior product designer and design engineer who works end-to-end, from problem framing and information architecture to production React. Led Playlist's first LLM product from pilot to 89% support deflection, and now leads design for its agentic AI platform.

Shaun works across the traditional boundaries of design, product, and engineering, owning problems end-to-end. Before designing software he was a frontend engineer at Castyr and a design researcher at Brown's Language and Thought Lab. He is drawn to how structures shape behavior and access, and thinks of software as the most important built environment we have today.

Highlights:

Promoted twice in 2.5 years; lead designer across three squads on a 25-year-old B2B platform serving 42,000 fitness and wellness businesses in 128 countries.
Led Playlist's first LLM product — a support assistant grown from a 500-studio pilot to ~120k conversations per quarter at 89% deflection, with a V2 interface built directly in code that lifted daily active users 26%.
Design lead for the agentic AI platform: modeled 23 use-case flows into 8 reusable conversational primitives and built the prototype and evaluation program that serve as its design spec.
Ships production React and TypeScript alongside engineers — a genuine design-engineer, not a designer who dabbles.
Settings modernization cut related support cases 38% year over year (1M+ searches, 178k monthly interactions).
Hackathon '25: 3rd of 41 teams for a Figma Code Connect and AI page-generation workflow, now a company priority.

Selected work:

Mindbody AI (Design Lead + Design Engineer, 2023 – active) — Zero-to-one design of Playlist's first LLM product — a support assistant grown from a 500-studio pilot into the front door of support for every customer (~120k conversations per quarter at 89% deflection; a V2 built directly in code lifted daily active users 26%) — now evolved into an agentic platform where any squad ships actions on one cohesive system.
Settings (Lead Designer, 2024) — A settings framework built on search. In-page navigation and search cut related support cases 38% year over year (1M+ searches, 178k monthly interactions); the table, side-nav, and flyout patterns became the squad's shared design system.
Appointment Setup (Lead Designer, 2025) — Ground-up redesign of Mindbody's most error-prone setup area. Flattened the page around the median customer's catalog and moved pricing and staff editing into a search-first side panel — cutting appointment-related support cases 22% and edit time 16%; its patterns seeded the design system.
Corporate Platform (Design Lead + Acting PM, 2026) — Design lead and acting PM for an 8-tool modernization of multi-location enterprise admin. Wrote the design principles and product gates the roadmap now cites, and shipped Pricing Options and Promotions across the corporate toolset.

For a fuller machine-readable briefing, see /llms.txt.

About me
A few things that set me apart
Previously

I do my best working across the traditional boundaries of design, product, and engineering. I like owning problems end-to-end, and believe that teams do better when constraints, details, and empathy are shared by everyone.

As a designer, I love to turn messy, frustrating things into tools and systems that people can trust, value, and actually enjoy using.

As an urban studies geek, I'm drawn to the way structures shape behavior, access, and possibility. I think of software as the most important built environment we have today: something we shape, and something that quietly shapes us back.

Before designing software, I was already designing and tinkering in many ways. Growing up, I modified RC cars, built my own Stratocaster, made posters, and wrote and produced music.

Studied computer science at Brown.

Worked as a frontend engineer at Castyr.

Researched psychology at the Brown Language and Thought Lab.

Consulted for technology companies through Brown Collegiate Consulting Group.

Started a platform connecting student organizations across schools with an incubator at Brown.

Studied jazz vocals under Daniela Schächter from Berklee.

Worked at a startup accelerator with early-stage founders.

Starting in support

This was initially built as a support assistant in 2023: a chat panel in Mindbody's navigation that answers customers' questions from our help center. We piloted it with 500 studios, rolled it out to every customer in early 2024, and that summer it replaced our old email support form.

Our AI support experience grew to become the front door of support for every Mindbody customer, creating significant cost savings for Playlist while unlocking more accurate, faster, personalized responses for customer issues.

Agentic workflows for onboarding and internal tools

Agentic actions

An organization-wide platform for agentic workflows

Agentic platform

Earlier this year, we decided to scale our assistant so that instead of just answering your questions, you can complete almost any action in Mindbody by asking. We'd realized it didn't have to only react: it could proactively help solve customers' issues, do things for them, and take a more pronounced role.

The intention behind the platform is to allow customers to complete nearly any complex task by chatting with an agent. As the sole designer, I defined the platform's fundamental building blocks and chat shell, supporting a cohesive experience that all squads can build their own actions and use cases on.

This work is ongoing.

about

How I became a developer, what I care about, and the experience I bring to a product team.

My journey into programming began in 2016. I was 14, learning Java and C++ by memorising small programs for exams. I did not understand much of the theory yet, but seeing a program run successfully gave me a reason to keep exploring.

That curiosity led me to a Diploma in Computer Engineering, where computers, networks, and software started to make sense as connected systems. In 2022, I built my first websites with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and SCSS, then published them by dragging the files into GitHub. It was a scrappy beginning, but it made building for the web feel real.

I joined a startup as an intern in 2023 and experienced how production software is designed, reviewed, and shipped. Alongside college, I spent the following year strengthening my fundamentals, learning modern web development, and building projects that pushed me beyond tutorials.

Today I work across frontend, backend, AI engineering, infrastructure, and system design. I care most about clarity, speed, accessibility, and the small interaction details that make a product trustworthy. I still approach every new build with the curiosity that started with my first Hello World.

observations.title: VoiceID - Juliette
observations.text:
Back
VoiceID

Sign in by just speaking

Active
Sep 2026
#voice
#python
#fastapi
#nextjs
GitHub ↗
Why

Passwords are the part of software nobody actually wants to think about, and they keep leaking. VoiceID is my attempt at a login with no password at all: an account is a username plus a voice. You record five short sentences once, and from then on signing in is reading one sentence into your microphone.

It's built on a real speaker recognition model, ECAPA-TDNN, running inside FastAPI, with the browser doing nothing but recording. I wrote three blog posts about it because the interesting work is mostly in the backend. The idea and frontend, the audio pipeline, and the verification itself.

VoiceID voice login page
How it works
Recording the five enrolment sentences, one prompt at a time
Record five short sentences at registration (different phrases each time, so the embeddings aren't near-duplicates)
Each upload goes through ffmpeg (downsampled to 16 kHz mono) and Silero VAD (speech detected and trimmed)
ECAPA-TDNN turns the cleaned audio into a 192-dimensional embedding
Login compares the live embedding to the stored set with cosine similarity, and passes when the score clears a threshold
No password, no email, no raw audio stored, the samples stay as vectors
VoiceID home page after a successful login
Details

Built with Python and FastAPI on the backend, serving the speaker model behind a single endpoint. Next.js handles the browser side and proxies everything to the API so the session stays same-origin. Vectors live in PostgreSQL with pgvector, sessions are opaque tokens stored only as SHA-256 hashes, and rate limiting plus per-username lockout sit in front of the login.

One honest caveat: this is speaker verification, not liveness. Replaying a recording of the enrolled voice will pass. It's a great login for a demo and a terrible one for a bank.

The whole flow end to end: register, then sign in with your voice
Tech Stack

Built with Python, FastAPI, and Next.js. The source is on GitHub.
